1	Accepted Manuscript
2	
3	Title: Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion
4	Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective
5	
6	Authors: Ryan T. Dech, Scott A. Bishop, J. Patrick Neary
7	
8	PII:                   S1440-2440(18)30867-3
9	DOI:                   https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2019.06.007
10	Reference:             JSAMS 2095
11	
12	To appear in:          Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
13	
14	Received date:         10 September 2018
15	Revised date:          20 May 2019
16	Accepted date:         21 June 2019
17	
18	Please cite this article as: Dech RT, Bishop SA, Neary JP, Why Exercise may be
19	Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective, Journal of Science
20	and Medicine in Sport (2019), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2019.06.007
21	
22	This is a PDF file of an unedited manuscript that has been accepted for publication.
23	As a service to our customers we are providing this early version of the manuscript.
24	The manuscript will undergo copyediting, typesetting, and review of the resulting proof
25	before it is published in its final form. Please note that during the production process
26	errors may be discovered which could affect the content, and all legal disclaimers that
27	apply to the journal pertain.
28	                                                                                                   1
29	
30	Title
31	
32	Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective
33	
34	
35	
36	Authors
37	
38	Ryan T. Dech, Scott A. Bishop, J. Patrick Neary
39	
40	                                                                 SC
41	Affiliations
42	                                                                   RI
43	Faculty of Kinesiology & Health Studies, University of Regina, Regina, SK, Canada, S4S 0A2
44	
45	                                                                     PT
46	Corresponding Author
47	                                                           U
48	J. Patrick Neary, PhD, Faculty of Kinesiology & Health Studies, University of Regina, Regina, SK,
49	
50	                                                    N
51	Canada, S4S 0A2. Email: Patrick.neary@uregina.ca; telephone 1-306-585-4844, fax: 1-306-585-
52	4854
53	
54	Abstract                                      A
55	       Concussion diagnosis and rehabilitation management has become a prevalent area of
56	                                      M
57	research, and yet, much is still unknown about these complex injuries. Historically, exercise
58	
59	
60	                              D
61	prescription post-concussion was conservatively used for rehabilitation due to the potential harmful
62	
63	
64	                   TE
65	effects that exercise can have on damaged neurons. However, there has been a shift to implement
66	
67	exercise earlier into recovery as several studies have demonstrated positive outcomes. To further
68	
69	
70	          EP
71	this clinical guideline, the evidence must continue to support these positive outcomes from an
72	
73	inductive and deductive physiologic approach (i.e., the clinical evidence aligned from a micro- to
74	
75	CC
76	macroscopic approach and vice versa).
77	
78	        Thus, this review aims to refresh the knowledge base surrounding concussion from both a
79	
80	A
81	neurometabolic and a broader physiological perspective, and will use gene expression as a vehicle
82	
83	to demonstrate why and how physical activity has the capacity to optimize recovery from a cellular
84	
85	perspective. Ideally, understanding the cellular perspective will help guide clinical management,
86	
87	and promote research into post-concussion exercise.
88	                                                                                                        2
89	
90	Keywords
91	
92	Trauma, Nervous System, Mild Head Injury, Acute Exercise, Physical Activity, Cellular
93	
94	Physiology
95	
96	
97	Introduction
98	
99	
100	                                                                     SC
101	        As per the most recent consensus statement on concussion in sport, the use of exercise as
102	
103	a potential rehabilitation tool is underscored following concussive injury1. Furthermore, classifying
104	
105	                                                                       RI
106	sport concussion is an unresolved issue as it can be viewed as part of a traumatic brain injury
107	
108	
109	                                                                         PT
110	spectrum or as a physiologically reversible injury1. Nonetheless, sport-related-concussion (SRC) is
111	
112	typically defined within the following parameters: 1) an injury that is sustained by a direct blow or
113	
114	
115	                                                              U
116	impulsive force that is transmitted to the head, 2) symptom onset and impairment that is short lived
117	
118	
119	                                                       N
120	and resolves spontaneously, 3) functional changes (but not structural changes) are typically
121	
122	
123	                                                A
124	observed, and 4) a range of signs and symptoms that typically resolves in a sequential course and
125	
126	may involve loss of consciousness 1. Unfortunately, less emphasis has been placed using physically
127	                                        M
128	active recovery as part of the rehabilitation process primary related to limited knowledge in this
129	
130	
131	                               D
132	area as it pertains to the intensity, duration, frequency and volume of exercise that is safe to perform,
133	
134	
135	                    TE
136	and the unknown consequences (if any) of exercise on the recovering brain. Furthermore, the
137	
138	literature is limited related to the cellular processes involved in exercise rehabilitation following
139	
140	
141	         EP
142	concussion.
143	
144	        Concussion management differences can also stem from inter-patient variation that may be
145	
146	CC
147	influenced by several factors including: age, gender, fitness, time since last exercise bout,
148	
149	pharmaceutical agents taken, lifestyle choices prior to a diagnostic assessment (e.g. caffeine,
150	
151	A
152	alcohol, and tobacco intake), anxiety, and even time of day 2–4. Ironically, most of these variables
153	
154	can also influence the response to exercise. Thus, managing and/or controlling these factors is
155	
156	critical for both developing a true understanding of severity and treatment, as well as for avoiding
157	
158	environmental and psychologic factors that confound clinical and physiologic assessments. These
159	                                                                                                  3
160	
161	potential confounds require nuanced interpretation of the data, such that the modality of exercise
162	
163	and the expected physiologic response can be known (and includes considering the above patient
164	
165	variation factors). Only after this degree of nuanced interpretation is mastered, can one finally
166	
167	consider the differences in how the injured brain is responding or how it might respond during
168	
169	recovery when an exercise intervention is applied.
170	
171	                                                                SC
172	        Furthermore, the above factors make it difficult to set a recovery timeline trajectory, and
173	
174	
175	                                                                  RI
176	predict how exercise will impact this timeline 5–7. Generally, health practitioners have acted
177	
178	conservatively for safety’s sake as one patient may be capable of much more stimulation, physical
179	
180	                                                                    PT
181	activity, and cognitive loading than another for a given set of presenting symptoms 2,7,8.
182	
183	Additionally, symptoms are very difficult to compare between individuals because of their relative
184	                                                          U
185	nature. Thus, an individualized exercise rehabilitation program is paramount to ensure safe
186	
187	recovery. 9,10                                       N
188	                                             A
189	        The underlying exercise-induced physiologic mechanisms were not detailed in the new
190	
191	                                      M
192	consensus guidelines, as these documents were systematic reviews that were intended to be used
193	
194	for guiding concussion management and future research 1,7,11–15. Hence, more physiologically-
195	                             D
196	focused studies on the impact of exercise during the early stages of concussion recovery are
197	
198	                   TE
199	warranted, as this will help build future consensus statements that may be more tailored to the
200	
201	pathophysiological changes that occur throughout concussion recovery 16,17,18 To better tailor
202	         EP
203	exercise prescription post-concussion, it will be critical to demonstrate at a cellular level how
204	
205	exercise-induced changes in key cellular pathways enhance the recovery process 1,19.
206	CC      Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to review how exercise (when introduced early post-
207	
208	injury) may be beneficial for concussion management. The focus herein will largely be on cellular
209	A
210	physiology, and will include the following topics: concussion pathophysiology and healthy gene
211	
212	and second messenger systems, and their relation to exercise and brain injury.
213	
214	
215	
216	Overview of Concussion Pathophysiology
217	                                                                                                   4
218	
219	        Forces applied to the head or body can cause shearing and stretching of neuronal cell bodies
220	
221	and axons, which alter the membrane and receptor structure at the site of injury 20. A compromised
222	
223	membrane promotes the ability of ions to move down their concentration gradients more freely
224	
225	(e.g., potassium (K+) efflux and both sodium (Na+) and calcium (Ca2+) influx). This change in ion
226	
227	flow and regulation results in both altered neuronal metabolism at the site of injury, and at
228	
229	                                                                 SC
230	secondary neurons. Moreover, mitochondrial dysfunction at the site of injury and at secondary
231	
232	
233	                                                                   RI
234	neurons leads to immediate and delayed glucose metabolism processes 21,22. The above changes to
235	
236	mitochondria and glucose metabolism can also influence cerebral blood flow processes at the site
237	
238	                                                                     PT
239	of injury and at secondary neuroanatomical locations 16,21,23. The reader is encouraged to review
240	
241	Figures 1 and 2 to further understand the processes associated with concussion pathophysiology.
242	                                                           U
243	        [Place Figure 1 here]                       N
244	                                              A
245	        [Place Figure 2 here]
246	                                      M
247	                                D
248	                   TE
249	        Ion dysregulation. One of the mechanisms which connects the site of injury to secondary
250	
251	
252	        EP
253	neurons is the indiscriminate release of glutamate, a neurotransmitter that results in increased N-
254	
255	methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor activity. These receptors allow calcium to move into the
256	
257	CC
258	intracellular side of a neuron. The en masse rise of intracellular calcium as a result of NMDA
259	
260	receptor activity uncouples glucose metabolism and neurovascular coupling (discussed below)21,24.
261	
262	A
263	Furthermore, the binding of glutamate to NMDA receptors results in the opening of potassium and
264	
265	intracellular voltage-gated channels found on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Both of these actions
266	
267	only further compromise the regulation of intracellular ion concentrations 21. Again, this
268	                                                                                                       5
269	
270	indiscriminate release of glutamate at secondary injury sites is mirrored at the primary site of injury
271	
272	by increased membrane permeability to all ions 21.
273	
274	            Energy dysregulation. Decreased intracellular ion regulation at primary and secondary
275	
276	neuronal sites can also affect a mitochondria’s ability to maintain the proton gradient required for
277	
278	adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthesis. This may shift glucose metabolism towards anaerobic
279	
280	                                                                    SC
281	glycolysis, and further strains the energy requirements needed to restore these large ionic shifts 25.
282	
283	
284	                                                                      RI
285	When mitochondria can no longer function as intended, the excitotoxic effect of the ions can lead
286	
287	to cellular apoptosis21. Moreover, the ability to restore ion balances across the neuronal membrane
288	
289	                                                                        PT
290	(and reverse the excitotoxic status of the neuron) may be a key factor for stratifying the brain injury
291	
292	into either a TBI (non-reversible cytotoxic damage and neuronal cell death), or a concussion 10,24.
293	                                                             U
294	While the mechanism ultimately has a large impact on outcome (concussion vs. TBI), the above-
295	
296	                                                       N
297	discussed physiology regarding the neurometabolic changes suggests that there may be a cellular
298	
299	                                                 A
300	“tipping point”. This reduced oxidative capacity can also be reflected through changes in gene
301	
302	                                         M
303	expression and transcription, (discussed in a later section) 22.
304	
305	            Structural dysregulation. At the site of injury, microtubules and membrane receptors are
306	                                 D
307	being recycled and reorganized with the intent to restore function, and thus promote ion regulation
308	14,26
309	                      TE
310	        . This is crucial as active transport proteins in the plasma membrane such as Ca2+-ATP pump,
311	
312	and the Na+/K+ ionic pump, will be saturated, and their efficacy will be limited by: 1) membrane
313	             EP
314	integrity, and 2) the amount of ATP energy stores available. Moreover, assuming that the level of
315	
316	excitotoxicity is reversible (i.e. concussion rather than TBI), the recovering neuron (be it at the site
317	CC
318	of injury or at a secondary location) is also exposed to decreased regulation of neurovascular
319	
320	coupling, which can also hinder ATP synthesis through decreased nutrient delivery 27.
321	A           Blood flow dysregulation. Neurovascular coupling (NVC) matches oxygen delivery to
322	
323	active tissues from a cellular to regional level via adjustments to capillary bed and pial artery
324	
325	smooth muscle tone 28,29. NVC is driven by fine-tuned regulation of numerous ions and molecules,
326	
327	including: calcium, potassium, ATP, guanosine triphosphate (GTP – similar to ATP), and nitric
328	                                                                                                        6
329	
330	oxide (NO) 21,30. Some of these molecules and ions have been discussed above, and the reader
331	
332	should now be familiar with how the post-concussion ion dysregulation can conceivably influence
333	
334	blood          flow          at          primary           and          secondary           locations17.
335	
336	
337	
338	Gene Expression & Metabolism in Concussion: “Downstream Downregulation”
339	
340	                                                                     SC
341	        The concussion-induced ionic dysregulation, energy crisis, and impaired neurovascular
342	
343	
344	                                                                       RI
345	coupling, have been discussed above. These previously discussed topics can potentially affect
346	
347	several proteins and second messenger pathways, which can also influence genetic expression. Of
348	
349	                                                                         PT
350	significant importance are brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), cyclic adenosine
351	
352	monophosphate (cAMP) response binding protein (CREB), peroxisome proliferator-activated
353	                                                              U
354	receptor gamma co-activator 1-alpha (PGC-1a), mammalian target of rapamyicin (mTOR), and
355	
356	                                                       N
357	more 21,31–35. These factors are all essential in facilitating neuroprotection and synaptic plasticity in
358	
359	                                                A
360	the brain, as well as overall cell efficiency and neuronal homeostasis 11,12,35–37. The below
361	
362	                                        M
363	subsections will focus on the following: the cellular physiology of exercise and neuroplasticity
364	
365	(broadly), how concussion results in changes to select proteins (BDNF, PGC-1a, and mTOR), and
366	                               D
367	how exercise can theoretically reverse concussion pathophysiology. The reader is encouraged to
368	
369	                    TE
370	view Figure 3 below to get an overview of some of the above proteins.
371	
372	
373	
374	         EP
375	[Place Figure 3 here]
376	CC
377	A       Exercise-induced neuronal changes – ion regulation. An acute bout of aerobic exercise
378	
379	will challenge the regulatory capacity for intracellular ion concentrations, as numerous post-
380	
381	synaptic NMDA receptors will be stimulated at an increased frequency and intensity. The exercise-
382	
383	induced increase in flow of extracellular calcium across the neuronal membrane (into the cytosol)
384	                                                                                                     7
385	
386	will be met with increased intracellular fluxes of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum 13,14,26,38.
387	
388	A simplified model which explains this from an exercise perspective is the concomitant presence
389	
390	of norepinephrine and glutamate. More specifically, the binding of norepinephrine to an adrenergic
391	
392	receptor activates membrane-bound G-proteins, which in turn activates phospholipase-C (PLC),
393	
394	and creates diacyl glycerol and inositol triphosphate (IP3) 38–40. The influx of extracellular calcium
395	
396	                                                                   SC
397	from the NMDA receptor, in conjunction with inositol triphosphate generated from the adrenergic
398	
399	
400	                                                                     RI
401	receptor, will enhance the release of calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum through both
402	
403	endoplasmic reticulum-bound voltage-gated calcium receptors, and the endoplasmic reticulum-
404	
405	                                                                       PT
406	bound inositol triphosphate receptors. This regional enhancement of calcium influx from the
407	
408	endoplasmic reticulum will stimulate other nearby endoplasmic reticulum-bound voltage gated
409	                                                            U
410	calcium receptors and create a retrograde calcium wave back to the soma where calcium-dependent
411	
412	                                                      N
413	transcription factors and second messengers can be activated (e.g. calmodulin, mitogen associated
414	
415	                                               A
416	protein kinase (MAPK), etc.) 38. Many of these transcription factors reinforce the capacity for ion
417	
418	                                       M
419	regulation through enhanced genetic expression, which is what is impaired when a concussion is
420	
421	sustained3,20,21.
422	                              D
423	         Exercise-induced neuronal changes – energy regulation. The enhancement in postsynaptic
424	
425	                    TE
426	NMDA, adrenergic, and endoplasmic reticulum receptor stimulation, will require enhanced glucose
427	
428	metabolism and ATP utilization. Once again, norepinephrine can be used as a simplified model
429	          EP

Title

Authors

Ryan T. Dech, Scott A. Bishop, J. Patrick Neary

Abstract                                      A
       Concussion diagnosis and rehabilitation management has become a prevalent area of
                                      M
research, and yet, much is still unknown about these complex injuries. Historically, exercise


                              D
prescription post-concussion was conservatively used for rehabilitation due to the potential harmful


                   TE
effects that exercise can have on damaged neurons. However, there has been a shift to implement

exercise earlier into recovery as several studies have demonstrated positive outcomes. To further


          EP
this clinical guideline, the evidence must continue to support these positive outcomes from an

inductive and deductive physiologic approach (i.e., the clinical evidence aligned from a micro- to

CC
macroscopic approach and vice versa).

        Thus, this review aims to refresh the knowledge base surrounding concussion from both a

A
neurometabolic and a broader physiological perspective, and will use gene expression as a vehicle

to demonstrate why and how physical activity has the capacity to optimize recovery from a cellular

perspective. Ideally, understanding the cellular perspective will help guide clinical management,

and promote research into post-concussion exercise.
                                                                                                        2

Keywords

Trauma, Nervous System, Mild Head Injury, Acute Exercise, Physical Activity, Cellular

Physiology


Introduction


                                                                     SC
        As per the most recent consensus statement on concussion in sport, the use of exercise as

a potential rehabilitation tool is underscored following concussive injury1. Furthermore, classifying

                                                                       RI
sport concussion is an unresolved issue as it can be viewed as part of a traumatic brain injury


                                                                         PT
spectrum or as a physiologically reversible injury1. Nonetheless, sport-related-concussion (SRC) is

typically defined within the following parameters: 1) an injury that is sustained by a direct blow or


                                                              U
impulsive force that is transmitted to the head, 2) symptom onset and impairment that is short lived


                                                       N
and resolves spontaneously, 3) functional changes (but not structural changes) are typically


                                                A
observed, and 4) a range of signs and symptoms that typically resolves in a sequential course and

may involve loss of consciousness 1. Unfortunately, less emphasis has been placed using physically
                                        M
active recovery as part of the rehabilitation process primary related to limited knowledge in this


                               D
area as it pertains to the intensity, duration, frequency and volume of exercise that is safe to perform,


                    TE
and the unknown consequences (if any) of exercise on the recovering brain. Furthermore, the

literature is limited related to the cellular processes involved in exercise rehabilitation following


         EP
concussion.

        Concussion management differences can also stem from inter-patient variation that may be

CC
influenced by several factors including: age, gender, fitness, time since last exercise bout,

pharmaceutical agents taken, lifestyle choices prior to a diagnostic assessment (e.g. caffeine,

A
alcohol, and tobacco intake), anxiety, and even time of day 2–4. Ironically, most of these variables

can also influence the response to exercise. Thus, managing and/or controlling these factors is

critical for both developing a true understanding of severity and treatment, as well as for avoiding

environmental and psychologic factors that confound clinical and physiologic assessments. These
                                                                                                  3

potential confounds require nuanced interpretation of the data, such that the modality of exercise

and the expected physiologic response can be known (and includes considering the above patient

variation factors). Only after this degree of nuanced interpretation is mastered, can one finally

consider the differences in how the injured brain is responding or how it might respond during

recovery when an exercise intervention is applied.

                                                                SC
        Furthermore, the above factors make it difficult to set a recovery timeline trajectory, and


                                                                  RI
predict how exercise will impact this timeline 5–7. Generally, health practitioners have acted

conservatively for safety’s sake as one patient may be capable of much more stimulation, physical

                                                                    PT
activity, and cognitive loading than another for a given set of presenting symptoms 2,7,8.

Additionally, symptoms are very difficult to compare between individuals because of their relative
                                                          U
nature. Thus, an individualized exercise rehabilitation program is paramount to ensure safe

recovery. 9,10                                       N
                                             A
        The underlying exercise-induced physiologic mechanisms were not detailed in the new

                                      M
consensus guidelines, as these documents were systematic reviews that were intended to be used

for guiding concussion management and future research 1,7,11–15. Hence, more physiologically-
                             D
focused studies on the impact of exercise during the early stages of concussion recovery are

                   TE
warranted, as this will help build future consensus statements that may be more tailored to the

pathophysiological changes that occur throughout concussion recovery 16,17,18 To better tailor
         EP
exercise prescription post-concussion, it will be critical to demonstrate at a cellular level how

exercise-induced changes in key cellular pathways enhance the recovery process 1,19.
CC      Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to review how exercise (when introduced early post-

injury) may be beneficial for concussion management. The focus herein will largely be on cellular
A
physiology, and will include the following topics: concussion pathophysiology and healthy gene

and second messenger systems, and their relation to exercise and brain injury.



Overview of Concussion Pathophysiology
                                                                                                   4

        Forces applied to the head or body can cause shearing and stretching of neuronal cell bodies

and axons, which alter the membrane and receptor structure at the site of injury 20. A compromised

membrane promotes the ability of ions to move down their concentration gradients more freely

(e.g., potassium (K+) efflux and both sodium (Na+) and calcium (Ca2+) influx). This change in ion

flow and regulation results in both altered neuronal metabolism at the site of injury, and at

                                                                 SC
secondary neurons. Moreover, mitochondrial dysfunction at the site of injury and at secondary


                                                                   RI
neurons leads to immediate and delayed glucose metabolism processes 21,22. The above changes to

mitochondria and glucose metabolism can also influence cerebral blood flow processes at the site

                                                                     PT
of injury and at secondary neuroanatomical locations 16,21,23. The reader is encouraged to review

Figures 1 and 2 to further understand the processes associated with concussion pathophysiology.

        [Place Figure 2 here]

                   TE

        EP

CC

A

14,26

                                                              U

                                                       N

                                                A

                                        M

(broadly), how concussion results in changes to select proteins (BDNF, PGC-1a, and mTOR), and
                               D

                                                                        PT
associated proteins and tau protein) reinforce the localization and structure of the postsynapse 43,44.

                                                              U

                                                       N

                                                 A

                                         M

expression can occur via second-messenger systems (i.e. activation of MAPK, phospholipase-C,
                                 D
phosphatidyl inositol triphosphate binding to its cytosolic receptor, and the activation of CREB)
11,12
                      TE

the synapse, and enhance the pre-synaptic release of glutamate-containing vesicles. The ability of
            EP

CC

A

                                                                   SC

                                                                     RI

discussed above interact with mTOR, including: phospholipase-C, phosphatidyl inositol

                                                                       PT

                                                             U
translation regulators 51. Ergo, mTOR (in conjunction with BDNF activity) plays a central role in

                                                      N
merging extracellular signals such as NMDA receptor activity49 with metabolic resources for

                                                A
catabolic and anabolic processes, and also facilitates gene transcription and protein translation 52.

                                        M
         It is also important to note that the PGC1a and mTOR pathways compete for control during

exercise and are dependent on the type of stress. When one of these pathways is activated, the other
                               D
pathway becomes blunted. To simplify, the inverse relationship between mTOR and PGC1a can

                    TE
somewhat be explained as resistance-exercise pathway activation (mTOR – protein synthesis) and

aerobic exercise pathway activation (PGC1a – mitochondrial biogenesis). However, though mTOR
         EP
and PGC1a are in competition it is clear that they both have strong connections to healthy gene

expression in neurons.
CC      It should now be clear that both mTOR and BDNF can contribute to ionic, metabolic, and

structural regulation through protein synthesis (mTOR) or through other second messenger systems
A
(BDNF). Moreover, the mechanisms by which exercise enhances these processes should now be

clear, and thus how exercise can help concussion recovery.

        Exercise-induced neuronal changes – neurovascular coupling. As a last note in this

section, NVC relies on potassium, calcium, GTP and nitric oxide (NO) signalling. Exercise
                                                                                                  10

enhances the regulation of these ions, and thus the regulation of NVC is also enhanced. Nitric oxide

is also influenced by cAMP, which again has implications for delivering oxygen to a neuron that

will have enhanced metabolic activity and protein synthesis. Thus, exercising for concussion

recovery will also help with regulating the match between cellular energy demands and nutrient

delivery.

                                                                  SC
Application of Exercise to Neuronal Damage
                                                                    RI
        By this juncture, it is hoped that the reader can understand that in order to have

                                                                      PT
neuroplasticity, there must be a matching of blood flow (i.e., nutrient delivery) to neuronal

metabolism. What is critical to note is that several human studies which have demonstrated that
                                                           U
NVC is compromised during concussion3,53,54. However, performing exercise has been shown to

                                                     N
promote recovery7,17,22. Thus, the notion that exercise may have a direct application to enhancing

                                               A
recovery from concussion is gaining acceptance1,5,7. And yet the question remains - how can

                                       M
exercise promote neurovascular recoupling, and help resolve a concussion-induced metabolic

crisis? After all, it has been commonly noted throughout several concussion consensus statements
                              D
that exercise can cause symptom exacerbation17.

                   TE
        The crux of this question has been repeatedly mentioned from a management standpoint –

the use of exercise and/or physical activity that does not elicit symptoms 17. Unfortunately, the
            EP
physiology that elicits these symptoms has not been well studied from a human “cellular

mechanism” point of view. A plausible hypothesis can be drawn by recalling that there remains a
CC
large cytosolic and mitochondrial concentration of calcium being sequestered that need to be

corrected 5,7,21. What remains elusive is how much capacity for intracellular ion regulation is
A
restored 72 hours post-injury, as this level of restoration can be applied to exercise, which further

promotes more ion regulation.

        This margin for intracellular ion regulation (and the associated energy reserve) will likely

occur under conditions of mild exercise, as recent research suggests that low intensity exercise can
                                                                                                    11

be performed safely. If one exerts beyond the exacerbation-threshold, symptoms such as headache

or pressure in head (amongst other symptoms, - physiological and psychological alike) may

manifest for an undetermined period of time. At a cellular level, if exercise intensity is increased

beyond this exacerbation-threshold, then there will be an increased oxidative stress within the cell,

and may ultimately lead to the activation of apoptotic pathways 5,20,31,55,56. Thus, mild exercise is

                                                                   SC
important and that increased intensity can be deleterious for recovery.


                                                                     RI
        To further connect the above sections to exercising at intensities below symptom

exacerbation, recall that epinephrine is a neurotransmitter strongly associated with exercise, and

                                                                       PT
that it will increase cAMP and CREB concentration levels via transmembrane and soluble adenyl

cyclase. cAMP will also promote the synthesis of nitric oxide 11,12,35,39,47,57. The presence of nitric
                                                             U
oxide will aide in delivery of nutrients so that this heightened energy need for ionic regulation is

                                                      N
met for the duration of the exercise bout. Moreover, CREB will increase the expression of BDNF

                                               A
and PGC-1a. Increasing the expression of these proteins will promote mitochondrial biosynthesis,

                                       M
organelle restructuring, and improve membrane integrity via microtubule regulation 13–15.

        While the above is technically a theoretical rationale, there have been some human studies
                               D
to corroborate this thinking that mild exercise is important for recovery and management 23,56,58.

                   TE
Most recently, Leddy et. al used the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test in patients who were

initially assessed at an average of 5 days post-injury and exercised until reaching symptom
         EP
exacerbation.   Patients were then instructed to perform home activity at 80% of the initial

assessment intensity, which was found to be more beneficial in time to recovery as compared to a
CC
stretching group59. Additional research has identified that performing exercise for 10 - 15 minutes

at 40 - 50% of heart rate maximum in untrained individuals, and 15 – 20 minutes at 60-70% of
A
heart rate maximum in trained individuals are good estimates for prescribing exercise post-initial

assessment. It is worth noting that maximal heart rate was estimated using the following formula:

208 – (0.7 x age)60. These estimates will help avoid the exercise-induced ventilation threshold,

which can result in hyperventilation, followed by cerebral vasoconstriction60.                Though
                                                                                                   12

inconclusive, there is evidence to suggest that higher exertion (i.e., moderate and greater) can have

a detrimental effect to recovery, and so does long-duration aerobic activity at lower intensity levels

(greater than 45 minutes). This is thought to be due to increased oxidative stress, increased cortisol

secretion, and impaired cerebral blood flow regulation, among other cardiovascular factors60.

        Indeed, it has been found through several studies that concussion results in a decreased

                                                                   SC
oxidative capacity, which consequently leads to a down regulation of BDNF 24. As an example, a

introduction of sub-symptom activity (i.e., below a symptom exacerbation threshold where ion

                                                A
regulation can still occur) can help cytoarchitectural stability, mitochondrial biosynthesis and

                                        M
neurovascular recoupling. These cellular processes may act in synergy with several others to

reverse the pathophysiological processes of a concussion.
                               D
        Additionally of note, high variability in symptom presentation post-injury due to

                    TE
stimulation, in combination with behaviour change (e.g., a high performance athlete becoming

suddenly sedentary) can cloud clinical understanding of severity. Said differently, reducing or
         EP
limiting an active individual can prove much more detrimental than originally thought 22. It must

also be noted that the high variability in symptom score and clinical challenges are also resultant
CC
of a gross under-and-over self-reporting issue that has been well documented. However, this is not

to discount the effect of rapid change from frequent exertion/activity to isolated rest that an athlete
A
may experience.

        Ultimately, there are several factors that are associated with neuronal health and synaptic

plasticity. In the acute phases of concussion, several pathways are blunted through sedentary

behavior and remain in a down-regulated state while at rest 32. Conversely, sub-symptom threshold
                                                                                                    14

physical activity has been found to be associated with enhanced signaling pathways, that mitigate

the effects of a concussion and optimize recovery and resolution 7,10,12,22. What was not discussed

herein, but is an area for future discussion is how sub-symptom activity can be physiologically

challenged by modifying different aspects of exercise (i.e. duration, time, modality, intensity etc).



Practical Implications                                              SC
                                                                      RI
- Exercise can be beneficial for recovering from sport concussion as exercise can amplify cellular

healing.

                                                                        PT
- Exercise can be harmful for recovering from sport concussion if exercise is too intense.

- Understanding the physiology of concussion recovery and why exercise can be both “good” or

“bad” may lead to improvements in recovery protocols.            U

 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised within-participant laboratory study in 13 well-trained young men who performed loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM under four eccentric tempos: 5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated (consecutive jumps).  "screeningLimitations": "This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, and no training adaptation was measured, so it cannot show whether fast eccentrics improve strength or power over time. The accelerated condition used consecutive jumps with no rest, whereas the other tempos had a 3-second rest, so the conditions differ in more than eccentric speed. The sample is resistance-trained men, not described as competitive athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as a rule that all loaded jumps should be braked as fast as possible for better training outcomes, when the study measured acute jump performance only and the accelerated tempo also changed rest.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Hernández-Davó JL, Sabido R, Omar-García M, Boullosa D. Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Influence of Eccentric Velocity on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps at Different Loads. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).",
   "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2023-0273",
   "abstract": "The study compared four eccentric tempos (5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated) on eccentric kinetics and kinematics and on the concentric performance of loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM in 13 well-trained participants.",
   "tldr": "In this single session, faster eccentric phases in loaded jumps increased end-eccentric work and jump velocity compared with a 5-second tempo. Treat this as a reason to trial fast eccentrics and monitor the result, not as a settled training rule.",
   "methods": "Randomised, within-participant repeated-measures design. Thirteen well-trained young men completed 12 sets (four eccentric tempos by three loads) of four loaded countermovement jumps after 1RM testing and two familiarisation sessions. Barbell kinematics and kinetics were recorded with a linear position transducer, and a two-way MANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests was used.",
   "findings": "The accelerated tempo produced greater total eccentric work than all other tempos at each load. Eccentric work in the last 100 ms was greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s tempo at each load. Peak and mean propulsive velocities were greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s tempo. Eccentric depth did not differ by tempo or load. In the accelerated condition, the change in end-eccentric work was strongly correlated with the change in concentric force (r above .77).",
   "limitations": "This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, with no training outcome. The accelerated condition used consecutive jumps without rest, unlike the other tempos, which confounds tempo with rest structure. The methods text refers once to a squat jump exercise, while the title, abstract and most of the text describe countermovement jumps.",
   "practicalImplications": "In this session, a fast or continuous eccentric phase in loaded jumps gave more eccentric work and higher jump velocity than a 5-second tempo. Whether this improves strength or power over a training block is not tested here, so trial it and monitor it rather than adopt it as a fixed rule.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Faster eccentric phases (fast or accelerated) raised end-eccentric work and jump velocity in well-trained men within one session. Coaches could trial fast eccentrics in loaded jumps, but the chronic effect on strength and power was not measured.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Not applicable. The study used healthy trained men and excluded those with joint injury in the prior 12 months, so it does not inform rehabilitation or return to sport."
 }
}

  Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Inﬂuence of Eccentric Velocity
   on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps
                       at Different Loads
             Jose L. Hernández-Davó,1,2 Rafael Sabido,2 Manuel Omar-García,2 and Daniel Boullosa3,4,5
     1
   Department of Health Sciences, Universidad Isabel I, Burgos, Spain; 2Department of Sports Sciences, Miguel Hernandez University of Elche, Elche, Spain;
 3
  Faculty of Physical Activity and Sports Sciences, Universidad de León, Leon, Spain; 4Integrated Institute of Health, Federal University of Mato Grosso do Sul,
                               Campo Grande, Brazil; 5College of Healthcare Sciences, James Cook University, Townsville, Australia

         Purpose: The aim of the present study was to analyze the effect of different eccentric tempos on eccentric kinetics and kinematics
         and the subsequent concentric performance when performing countermovement jumps against different loads. Methods: After
         1-repetition-maximum assessment and 2 familiarization sessions, 13 well-trained participants performed, in randomized order,
         12 sets (4 tempos × 3 loads) of 4 repetitions of the loaded countermovement-jump exercise. The eccentric tempos analyzed were 5
         and 2 seconds, as fast as possible, and accelerated (ie, without pause between repetitions), while the loads used were 30%, 50%,
         and 70% of 1-repetition maximum. Several kinetic and kinematic variables during both phases were recorded by linking a linear
         position transducer to the barbell. Results: The eccentric work was greater in the accelerated condition despite no changes in the
         eccentric depth. The peak and mean propulsive velocities were greater in the as-fast-as-possible and accelerated conditions.
         Correlation analysis showed that, compared with the 5-second condition, the increased concentric performance in the accelerated
         condition was related to the difference in eccentric work performed in the last 100 milliseconds of the eccentric phase (r > .770).
         Conclusions: Contrary to current practices, the current study highlights the need for performing the eccentric phase of loaded
         countermovement jumps, a common exercise performed by athletes for both training and evaluation purposes, as fast as possible.
         This allows not only a greater eccentric work but also improved concentric performance.

         Keywords: stretch-shortening cycle, muscle power, athletic performance, velocity-based training, force–velocity proﬁle

 "id": "Q74",
 "sourceFile": "Why sports should embrace bilateral asymmetry - A narrative review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Why Sports Should Embrace Bilateral Asymmetry: A Narrative Review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of bilateral (interlimb) asymmetry in sport, covering its occurrence, its relationship with performance, its link to injury, and the effect of training on it. The authors report that asymmetry is common across sports, ages, sexes and competitive levels, is task- and time-dependent and poorly correlated with performance, and that no evidence shows pre-existing asymmetry raises injury risk or that reducing asymmetry improves performance.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. Many cited asymmetry studies use single tests or test-retest designs, and sport-specific performance assessments are mostly lacking, as the review itself notes. The no-harm conclusion therefore relies partly on absence of evidence.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as saying asymmetry never matters, when it says asymmetry is poorly understood for sport-specific performance and that injuries tend to increase it.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2022,
   "citation": "Afonso J, Peña J, Sá M, Virgile A, García-de-Alcaraz A, Bishop C. Why Sports Should Embrace Bilateral Asymmetry: A Narrative Review. Symmetry. 2022;14:1993.",
   "doi": "10.3390/sym14101993",
   "abstract": "The paper critically reviews the evidence on the occurrence of bilateral asymmetry in sport and its effects on sports performance, injury risk and training, and it argues against assumptions that asymmetry is harmful.",
   "tldr": "Bilateral asymmetry is common in sport and does not appear to impair performance or raise injury risk. Asymmetry scores fluctuate a lot, so judge them over repeated tests rather than from a single result.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of the literature on bilateral asymmetry in sport, organised around occurrence and performance, injury, and training effects. The text does not describe a systematic search.",
   "findings": "Asymmetry is prevalent across several sports regardless of age, sex or competitive level, and can appear even in apparently symmetric actions such as running and rowing. Asymmetry measures are task-, metric- and sport-specific, fluctuate in size and direction over time, and correlate poorly with each other and with performance. Injuries tend to accentuate asymmetry, but pre-existing asymmetry has not been shown to increase injury risk. Training programmes can reduce asymmetry, but the review finds no evidence that this improves sport-specific performance or reduces injury risk.",
   "limitations": "The review is narrative, with no described search, so study selection is not reproducible. Sport-specific performance assessments are mostly lacking, and many cited studies use single tests or test-retest data. The conclusion that asymmetry is not harmful relies partly on absence of evidence.",
   "practicalImplications": "Do not treat one asymmetry score as a problem to correct. Because asymmetry measures fluctuate, use group means and repeated measures, and do not assume that reducing asymmetry improves performance or lowers injury risk.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Asymmetry is common in athletes and the review argues against targeting symmetry for its own sake. Track interlimb differences across repeated tests and judge them against performance outcomes rather than a fixed symmetry target.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review notes that injuries tend to increase asymmetry, but it does not show that pre-existing asymmetry raises injury risk. It cannot be used to set return-to-play symmetry thresholds, because it does not test any clearance criteria."
 }
}

Asymmetry measures are task-, metric- and sport-specific, fluctuate in size and direction over time, and correlate poorly with each other and with performance. Injuries tend to accentuate asymmetry, but pre-existing asymmetry has not been shown to increase injury risk. Training programmes can reduce asymmetry, but the review finds no evidence that this improves sport-specific performance or reduces injury risk.",
   "limitations": "The review is narrative, with no described search, so study selection is not reproducible. Sport-specific performance assessments are mostly lacking, and many cited studies use single tests or test-retest data. The conclusion that asymmetry is not harmful relies partly on absence of evidence.",
   "practicalImplications": "Do not treat one asymmetry score as a problem to correct. Because asymmetry measures fluctuate, use group means and repeated measures, and do not assume that reducing asymmetry improves performance or lowers injury risk.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Asymmetry is common in athletes and the review argues against targeting symmetry for its own sake. Track interlimb differences across repeated tests and judge them against performance outcomes rather than a fixed symmetry target.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review notes that injuries tend to increase asymmetry, but it does not show that pre-existing asymmetry raises injury risk. It cannot be used to set return-to-play symmetry thresholds, because it does not test any clearance criteria."
 }
}
