77	                                 This search for bilateral symmetry (which includes bilateral trunk asymmetries and
78	                          also interlimb asymmetries) seems to derive more from deeply held beliefs than from
79	                          empirical findings [14], and risks placing performance and injury prevention programs on
80	                          the wrong track. Incidentally, craniocaudal and dorsoventral asymmetries are promptly
81	                          accepted (i.e., people understand that we need one head on top and two feet on the bottom,
82	                          and that we have two eyes in front of the head but none in the back). Somehow, it is with
83	                          bilateral asymmetry in sport that some in our profession seem to struggle to appreciate.
84	                          However, there is hope: the 10th edition of the ACSM guidelines for exercise testing and
85	                          prescription makes no mention of symmetry in general exercise prescription [15], unlike
86	                          the 9th edition [16]. Across the entire 10th edition of the guidelines, the only reference
87	                          to symmetry is the suggestion of symmetrical and rhythmical movement for people with
88	                          athetoid cerebral palsy [15].
89	                                 Biologically, the healthy development of human embryos requires breaking several
90	                          symmetries, including dorsoventral and craniocaudal [17]; unsurprisingly, proper embry-
91	                          ologic developmental also requires breaking left–right symmetry in vertebrates, including
92	                          humans [17–21]. Consequently, human anatomy is abundant with bilateral asymmetries.
93	                          Despite an apparent external symmetry, there is considerable asymmetry in thoracic and
94	                          abdominal organs [19,21]. For example, the diaphragm is asymmetric, usually reaching
95	                          one rib higher on the right side (due to the influence of the liver) and one lumbar vertebra
96	                          lower on the right side (due to a longer pillar) [22]. The aorta (which is also asymmetric)
97	                          presses against the vertebral column and usually produces a slight thoracic curvature with
98	                          convexity towards the right side [22]. Many other asymmetries can be pinpointed with
99	                          respect to internal organs (e.g., the liver, heart, lungs, colon, pancreas, etc.), which are all
100	                          commonly known. However, there are many additional bilateral asymmetries in vascular
101	                          networks, the lymphatic drainage system, and neural pathways [22]. In some cases, nerves
102	                          not only traverse distinct paths on the right and the left side of the body, but they also
103	                          present histological differences, such as in the case of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in
104	                          humans [23,24].
105	                                 Importantly, bilateral anatomical asymmetries in humans extend to the upper and
106	                          lower limbs as well (e.g., widths, lengths, neuromuscular paths, the different number
107	                          of muscle bellies, and among many other features) and have been widely described in
108	                          the literature [22,25–29]. A recent review has synthesized interlimb asymmetries in the
109	                          hamstrings’ structure and functionality, highlighting that important intraindividual asym-
110	                          metries may exist (some of which are not changeable with training) [30]. Naturally, laterality
111	                          (i.e., a lateral preference for using one limb over the other in certain tasks) coupled with
112	                          interlimb anatomical asymmetries suggests that common activities such as walking and
113	                          running should result in significant interlimb asymmetries in gait (kinetic and kinematic) in
114	                          healthy populations and athletes [31–33], and that sports may actually require magnifying
115	                          certain asymmetries [14,34] (e.g., sports with highly unilaterally-biased actions).
116	                                 Given all the above, asymmetry seems to be part of nature and integral to human
117	                          biology and behavior. In sports, interlimb asymmetries are highly task- and metric-
118	                          specific [7,11,12,14,34–43] and so should be analyzed within proper context. The goal
119	                          of this narrative review was to provide an account on the role of asymmetry in sports,
120	                          focusing on its relationships with performance and injury occurrence. We chose to perform
121	                          a narrative review to deliver a broad and critical overview of these topics, focusing on key
122	                          concepts and trying to tell a compelling story.
123	
124	                          2. Bilateral Asymmetry Is Ubiquitous in Sports Performance
125	                               Bilateral asymmetry (a broad term referring to bilateral trunk asymmetries or inter-
126	                          limb asymmetries) should be expected to be and is (probably) not even clinically relevant
127	                          below the arbitrary thresholds of 5–15% [5,7,11,44–47], with an emphasis on the arbitrari-
128	                          ness of such thresholds since they are task- and metric-specific [7,11,12,34–39,42,48–50]
129	 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                             3 of 18
130	
131	
132	
133	
134	                          and likely also individual-specific [42,49–53]. Laterality (including, but not limited to,
135	                          handedness, mastication, and eye dominance) is a well-established feature in the animal
136	                          kingdom, including humans, and has been shown to be associated with increased func-
137	                          tional performance [54–59]. Importantly, both limb dominance and preference may also be
138	                          task-specific [34]. Therefore, interlimb asymmetries should not be automatically associated
139	                          with performance impairments [14,36,60]. Team sports such as basketball, handball, or vol-
140	                          leyball, to name some notorious examples, may boost upper limb asymmetries due to their
141	                          highly specialized and differentiated demands, and the same could be said of racquet sports
142	                          such as tennis, padel, or badminton. In the case of the lower limbs, bilateral asymmetries
143	                          are the norm in both general populations and in athletes [12]. For example, in 38 male
144	                          adult soccer players, resting tensiomyography assessments showed significant interlimb
145	                          asymmetries [61]. The vastus medialis contraction time, rectus femoris sustained time and
146	                          half-relaxation time, and biceps femoris sustained time were greater in the dominant limb,
147	                          while vastus lateralis contraction time and delay time were greater in the non-dominant
148	                          limb [61].
149	                               Moreover, we should consider the “noisy” character of asymmetry and the inconsis-
150	                          tency of outcomes, whereby in test–retest studies the group mean asymmetry often appears
151	                          to be relatively stable, but the standard deviation (SD) of the mean is almost always very
152	                          large (i.e., 50–100% of the mean asymmetry value) [38,49,52,62]. In contrast to the mean,
153	                          when individual datapoints are considered, changes in asymmetry’s magnitude and direc-
154	                          tion are usually quite large [38,39,49,50,52,53,62–66], suggesting caution when interpreting
155	                          the mean value of any interlimb asymmetry data. In fact, interlimb asymmetries should
156	                          not even be considered “true” asymmetries if their value is equal to or smaller than the
157	                          inherent variability of any given test [42,53] (e.g., coefficient of variation and typical error
158	                          of measurement). Additionally, limb preference and limb dominance are not necessarily
159	                          coincident; we refer the readers to the work of Virgile and Bishop [34] for an exploration
160	                          of this topic. To truly elucidate the relevance of asymmetry in sports performance, we
161	                          must understand: (1) the occurrence and relationships of bilateral asymmetry with athletic
162	                          performance, and (2) the effects of training interventions on interlimb asymmetries.
163	
164	                          2.1. Occurrence and Relationship of Bilateral Asymmetry with Athletic Performance
165	                                A recent systematic review showed that, among several populations (including
166	                          17 studies with athletes), inter-limb strength asymmetries ranged from near symmetry
167	                          to asymmetries larger than 15%, without clear relationships with independent performance
168	                          tasks (such as isokinetic dynamometry, jump tests, and seated shot put, among others) [46].
169	                          Furthermore, additional research has shown that in sports research, no clear-cut associa-
170	                          tions exist between bilateral asymmetries and performance [14]. In addition, any findings
171	                          from cross-sectional studies should be taken with a pinch of salt, since the relationships
172	                          between interlimb asymmetry (magnitude and direction) and performance are not neces-
173	                          sarily consistent across a sports season [34,39,42,63,64,67]. One study assessed the ground
174	                          reaction forces (GRF) of 13 plyometrics-trained subjects (23 ± 3 years, 8 male and 5 female)
175	                          after a 45-cm drop jump whereby the subjects had to change their lead leg (i.e., the leg
176	                          initiating the movement to step off the box) [1]. Upon landing, the lead leg generated
177	                          greater forces than the trail leg. Interestingly, pairwise comparisons showed that significant
178	                          interlimb differences occurred only when the right leg led the movement, with the right
179	                          leg making earlier ground contact and generating greater force and impulse than the left
180	                          leg. Limb symmetry indices (LSI) generally showed asymmetries ≥10% [1]. This shows
181	                          that even in a simple drop jump task (with low contextual interference), athletes exhibit
182	                          marked interlimb asymmetry in their performance. However, the drop jump height was not
183	                          assessed, and so it is unclear how the observed asymmetries impacted jump performance.
184	                                In high-level male (n = 38) and female judokas (n = 23), the maximum isometric
185	                          strength of the shoulder external rotators was significantly superior (albeit with a small
186	                          effect size of η2 = 0.03) in the dominant side in comparison with the non-dominant side, but
187	                          the same was not observed for internal rotation [4]. Asymmetries favoring the dominant
188	 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                              4 of 18
189	
190	
191	
192	
193	                          side were also detected for the unilateral seated shot put test (small effect, η2 = 0.07), but not
194	                          for the Y balance test [4]. In summary, upper limb dominance (i.e., a bilateral asymmetry)
195	                          seemed to affect the performance of shoulder external rotations and unilateral seated
196	                          shot put, but the effects were very small. In 26 male handball players (U18), interlimb
197	                          asymmetry across a variety of jump and change-of-direction (COD) tests ranged from ~3.7
198	                          to ~12.7% [41]. Moderately significant correlations (ρ = 0.41–0.51) were found between
199	                          isoinertial crossover step asymmetry (but not lateral shuffle step) and a COD of 90◦ and
200	                          COD of 180◦ in both limbs, as well as 20 m sprinting. However, interlimb asymmetries were
201	                          also quantified in the several single leg jumps and COD tests, which were independent of
202	                          performance [41].
203	                                In a study involving young elite tennis players (n = 41; ~50% females) and sex- and
204	                          age-matched controls (n = 41), significant asymmetries were registered in both groups
205	                          across all seven upper and lower limb tests [68], which broadly assessed strength, reaction
206	                          time, and COD. While tennis players were significantly more asymmetric than the controls
207	                          with respect to handgrip strength, they were less asymmetric than the controls in the
208	                          single leg countermovement jump (CMJ) and 6 m single leg hop tests. These asymmetries
209	                          were test-specific and, since the different tests were not examined for possible correlations,
210	                          it is unclear how asymmetric performance in one test could have affected a different test.
211	                          Significant interlimb morphological asymmetries (e.g., circumferences and widths) were
212	                          also found for both tennis players and the controls, although these were significantly higher
213	                          in the tennis players for the upper limbs (but not the lower limbs), which is to be expected
214	                          given the nature of the sport [68]. Moreover, the data from that study suggested that both
215	                          morphological and functional asymmetries were not significantly related to each other (i.e.,
216	                          the morphological asymmetries did not affect performance in the strength and COD-related
217	                          tests) and should best be interpreted independently [68]. Similar results were found by the
218	                          same research group for a different sample of 22 high-level female tennis players [69].
219	                                When performing the volleyball spike (which is a highly asymmetric action, both for
220	                          the lower and upper limbs), a systematic review showed that attackers landed asymmetri-
221	                          cally >65% of times, mostly on the left leg, and significant interlimb kinematic asymmetries
222	                          were noted for the ankle, knee, and hip joints upon landing (e.g., joint flexion angle, range
223	                          of motion, maximal flexion velocity, and angle upon initial contact with floor) [70]. Even in
224	                          highly controlled experimental settings where the athletes were explicitly asked to land
225	                          on both feet simultaneously [71–73], a unilateral landing was still the norm. Therefore,
226	                          asymmetric landing strategies seem to be preferred in volleyball [70]. Even in supposedly
227	                          more symmetric actions such as blocking, players have been shown to be faster moving
228	                          towards the right side than to the left side of the court even in highly-controlled tasks
229	                          with reduced contextual interference [74]. However, it is currently unclear how these
230	                          asymmetries are related to performance outcomes, such as attack or block jump height.
231	                          Further, it is unknown whether volleyball players’ landing asymmetries are associated with
232	                          a positive, neutral, or negative effect on the performance of these key game actions.
233	                                In soccer, interlimb asymmetries ranging from −11.01 ± 12.38% (U18) to −18.43 ± 12.11%
234	                          (U16) have been observed in 68 soccer players when performing 90◦ COD tasks [75]. Note
235	                          the very large SDs, indicating a large within-group variability. The COD time was signifi-
236	                          cantly lower for the dominant than for the non-dominant side (no effect size available) [75].
237	                          In addition, in soccer, a study of 46 male professional players (26 ± 6 years of age) ver-
238	                          ified 8.4 ± 6.6% and 9.0 ± 7.1% interlimb asymmetries in isometric maximal voluntary
239	                          contraction (MVC) torque and isokinetic knee peak extension torque. These interlimb
240	                          asymmetries were smaller than those registered for the rate of early, intermediate, late, and
241	                          peak torque development (RTD), which ranged from 12.3 ± 9.9% to 20.6 ± 14.3% (note
242	                          the very large SDs) [8]. However, the only asymmetries that were significantly correlated
243	                          (albeit weakly, i.e., ρ ≤ 0.36) with the International Knee Documentation Committee and
244	                          the Lysholm knee-scoring scales were early and intermediate RTD [8], denoting that the
245	                          different asymmetries were largely independent from performance.
246	 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                             5 of 18
247	
248	
249	
250	
251	                                In 16 male soccer players (14.7 ± 0.2 years), no significant relationships were observed
252	                          between interlimb asymmetry (single-leg Abalakov test, 10 m (5 + 5) and 20 m (10 + 10)
253	                          COD, and isoinertial power test) and performance tests (10, 20, and 30 m sprints plus
254	                          CMJ) [43]. The average interlimb asymmetries varied from 3.02 ± 1.74 % (20 m COD) and
255	                          21.68 ± 18.85% (peak power in the isoinertial test), but there were very large interindividual
256	                          variabilities (e.g., 0.14 to 57.37% in peak power in the isoinertial test) [43]. Another soccer-
257	                          related study followed 18 male U23 players for one season [67]. During both the preseason
258	                          and midseason, no significant relationships were found between interlimb asymmetries
259	                          and performance in sprint and COD tests, nor were there significant correlations between
260	                          changes in asymmetry and changes in sprint and COD performance across the entire
261	                          season [67]. In the authors’ own words, “suggestions for the reduction of asymmetry that
262	                          may indirectly enhance athletic performance cannot be made” (p. 787) [67].
263	                                In young female basketball players (n = 29, 15.7 ± 1.34 years of age), significant inter-
264	                          limb differences were identified for all neuromuscular tasks (single leg CMJ in different
265	                          directions, star excursion balance test (SEBT), and sprint with a COD) [35]. There was poor
266	                          agreement (35 to 52%) between the more skilled lower limb and the limb subjectively iden-
267	                          tified as being the dominant limb, which supports previous suggestions about differences
268	                          between limb dominance and limb preference [34]. While the bilateral asymmetry indices
269	                          between the more and less skillful limbs varied from 3.33 ± 2.49% (lateral CMJ distance)
270	                          and 14.11 ± 8.62% (vertical CMJ height) [35], the authors did not assess the correlations
271	                          between the magnitudes of asymmetry and the test performances. Therefore, while there
272	                          were bilateral asymmetries in performance in each test, it is unknown if asymmetries in one
273	                          test correlated with performance in another test, i.e., if the asymmetries were task-specific
274	                          or translated into more general performance.
275	                                Another study involving 11 female basketball players (U19) performed several tests
276	                          (10 m sprint, COD 90◦ , COD 135◦ , and single leg CMJ in three directions) plus four
277	                          exercises on a flywheel machine (acceleration step, deceleration step, crossover step, and
278	                          sidestep) [50]. Significant interlimb asymmetries were shown for all the tests, ranging from
279	                          1.26 ± 0.94 % (COD 135◦ ) to 11.75 ± 7.79% (vertical single-leg CMJ). The authors correlated
280	                          the interlimb asymmetry scores in the flywheel exercises (four exercises, both in concentric
281	                          and eccentric forms, in a total of eight conditions) and the performance with respect to
282	                          COD and unilateral jumps for both the highest and lowest performing limbs (in a total
283	                          of 14 conditions). Significant correlations (ρ = −0.61 to 0.81) were found for only 5 of the
284	                          112 cells (i.e., combinations) [50], all of which referred to correlations with the concentric
285	                          sidestep. When correlating interlimb asymmetry scores in the COD and unilateral jump
286	                          tests with the flywheel exercises, no significant correlations were found. By and large,
287	                          interlimb asymmetries were, therefore, not correlated with performance tests.
288	                                One study compared 18 professional male soccer players to 23 professional cricket
289	                          players with respect to performing single-leg CMJ and drop jumps, a 10 m sprint, and
290	                          a 505 COD [76]. The cricket athletes had significantly greater interlimb asymmetries
291	                          in jump height (11.49% vs. 6.51%) and in the reactive strength index (RSI; 10.37% vs.
292	                          5.95%) than the soccer players [76], suggesting that interlimb asymmetries may also be
293	                          sport-specific (i.e., certain sports may promote enhanced asymmetries due to their specific
294	                          performance demands). While these asymmetries in jump height and RSI were moderately
295	                          correlated with slower 505 COD times in the cricket players (r = 0.56–0.74), they were not
296	                          correlated with other performance tests [76]. No significant correlations between interlimb
297	                          asymmetries and performance tests were found for the soccer players [76].
298	                                Kinetic and kinematic interlimb asymmetries are frequent even in cyclic, bilateral
299	                          actions such as running and cycling [31–33,77]. In U15 swimmers (n = 38; half female), the
300	                          direction of asymmetry (i.e., favoring one limb or the other) was rarely consistent between
301	                          single-leg CMJ and single-leg standing long jump performances [78]. This implies that
302	                          the assessment of interlimb asymmetries may be highly task-specific, in line with other
303	                          works [7,8,11,12,35–38,43,50,63,67]. The asymmetry scores were not significantly different
304	                          between males and females and were not associated with 25 m and 50 m front crawl
305	 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                            6 of 18
306	
307	
308	
309	
310	                          swimming performance [78]. Considering the means plus the SDs, the asymmetry levels
311	                          were roughly within the previously mentioned 10–15% range [78]. However, it should be
312	                          noted that a recent review underlined the large SDs present in many symmetry-related
313	                          studies, suggesting that important interindividual variability almost always exists [11]. This
314	                          may partly explain why relationships between bilateral asymmetry (noisy and fluctuating)
315	                          and performance (more stable) are often weak or negligible.
316	                                The kinematic and kinetic joint parameters were assessed in 10 elite-level male rowers
317	                          on a rowing ergometer [7]. An average of 5–10% interlimb asymmetry was observed when
318	                          assessing the kinematic parameters of the ankle and the kinetic parameters of the hip
319	                          and knee joints (i.e., accelerations) [7]. Asymmetries > 10% were observed for the kinetic
320	                          ankle parameters, including resultant force and ankle joint acceleration [7]. In this study,
321	                          the kinetic asymmetries were uncorrelated with kinematic asymmetries and with lower
322	                          limb length asymmetry [7], further contributing to the notion that asymmetry assessments
323	                          may be task- and metric-specific [7,8,11,12,35–39,41,43,53,65]. The authors proposed that
324	                          a low inter-stroke variability in asymmetry could provide a more stable and efficient
325	                          performance [7]. The inter-stroke variability was said to be associated with 5–10% interlimb
326	                          asymmetries with respect to the acceleration of the hip and knee joints and in the ankle
327	                          joint angle, as well as with >10% asymmetries in the resultant force and in the acceleration
328	                          of the ankle joint [7], but no values were provided to corroborate these claims.
329	                                In artistic gymnastics, all beam routines of the qualification round (19 gymnasts) of the
330	                          B World Cup ’2014 were analyzed [79]: the right lower limb initiated 42.3% of all actions,
331	                          the left limb 29.1%, and both limbs 28.6%, denoting the asymmetric/lateral preferences
332	                          of top-level gymnasts. Moreover, 60% of the actions on the beam implied a unilateral
333	                          take-off and/or landing [79]. An analysis of six high-level female artistic gymnasts showed
334	                          significant kinetic and kinematic interlimb asymmetries in the upper limbs upon contact
335	                          with the floor when performing the forward handspring on floor [80]. However, in both
336	                          studies [79,80], the ways in which these asymmetries related to performance were not
337	                          reported. In summary, asymmetries appear to be the norm in sports, but we need a
338	                          deeper understanding of how they relate to performance in different tests. As the evidence
339	                          presented herein shows, the relationship between performance in standardized tests and
340	                          sports-specific performance is often missing in the available literature to date.
341	
342	                          2.2. Effects of Training Interventions to Reduce Bilateral Asymmetries in Sports
343	                                The previous section illustrated that bilateral asymmetry seems to be the norm in
344	                          sports. If a training program aims to reduce bilateral asymmetries (most commonly, inter-
345	                          limb asymmetries), how successful is it? A study aimed to reduce interlimb asymmetries in
346	                          24 male adult soccer players (amateur level) [13]. The participants were randomized into a
347	                          6-week (twice weekly) unilateral strength- and power-training program or into a control
348	                          group. Despite the experimental group having improved performance, the interlimb asym-
349	                          metry was unchanged for the 505 COD test and two of the three jump tests (single-leg CMJ
350	                          and single-leg broad jump) [13]. There was a moderate reduction in interlimb asymmetry
351	                          in the single-leg drop jump stiffness (g = 1.11) and RSI (g = 1.00) [13]. Another random-
352	                          ized study compared an 8-week (twice weekly) strength- and power-training program
353	                          (focused on the lower limbs and trunk) with controls in 37 female U17 soccer players [81].
354	                          The intervention resulted in no meaningful differences in interlimb asymmetries from
355	                          pre- to post-testing [81]. Similar results were found with a comparable sample of female
356	                          soccer players (n = 36; U14), albeit with a slightly longer intervention (twice weekly for
357	                          10 weeks) [82].
358	                                A non-randomized study with 20 adult male soccer players compared a 6-week core
359	                          stability training regimen with controls performing a “standard” warm-up [83], consisting
360	                          of jogging, dynamic stretching, and mobility [83]. The interlimb asymmetries in single-leg
361	                          CMJ were reduced after the training program for the “core” training group, but increased in
362	                          the controls, while no differences in interlimb asymmetry were observed for isokinetic knee
363	                          testing [83]. Given the details of the actual “core” training regimen that was implemented,
364	 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                             7 of 18
365	
366	
367	
368	
369	                          it is possible to speculate that the reductions in asymmetry in the jump tests may have
370	                          come from the weaker limb gaining strength and have nothing to do with core stability.
371	                          Moreover, the SDs shown in table V of the original study [83] are surprisingly small in
372	                          comparison with most other studies on the topic.
373	                                In 34 male handball players (U17), an 8-week randomized intervention compared the
374	                          effects of isoinertial and cable-resistance training on interlimb asymmetries [84]. Interlimb
375	                          asymmetry was reduced in only one of the eight performance tests (unilateral CMJ) [84].
376	                          In 22 U16 to U19 basketball players, a randomized study compared unilateral and bilateral
377	                          resistance training for 6 weeks [85]. Both groups improved in the performance tests such
378	                          as the CMJ and 25 m sprint, among others. Only the unilateral group showed reduced
379	                          interlimb asymmetries (no effect size provided) as assessed by the bilateral difference in the
380	                          maximum power in an incremental unilateral squat test [85]. However, the standardized
381	                          between-group differences crossed zero (i.e., there was no significant direction of the
382	                          effects) [85], even while applying 90% confidence limits, which are narrower than the more
383	                          common 95% limits. A randomized 8-week (twice a week) strength-training program was
384	                          contrasted with a volume-equated sport-specific training regimen in 31 male volleyball
385	                          players (aged 14.5 ± 0.5 years) [86]. Despite significant changes in performance (dynamic
386	                          balance test, single leg hop, CMJ, and back squat one repetition maximum), no differences
387	                          were observed with respect to interlimb asymmetry as assessed by the single-leg hop
388	                          tests [86].
389	                                A randomized study with U12 male weightlifters applied a 6-week (twice weekly)
390	                          hamstring eccentric training program versus controls; no changes in interlimb asymmetry
391	                          (derived from bilateral differences in the performance of the single leg hop test) were noted
392	                          from pre- to post-intervention [87]. In a randomized study with twenty-three U14 tennis
393	                          players (male and female), one group performed 12 sessions (two sessions per week over
394	                          6 weeks) focused on balance training, while the other group performed only tennis-specific
395	                          drills for the same period [88]. The lower limb bilateral asymmetries were significantly
396	                          reduced in the balance-training group only for the three tests that were performed (single-
397	                          leg hop, side-hop and side steps, and forward 4.115 m test [4m-SSF]) [88], but there was no
398	                          assessment of the effect size to quantify the magnitude of the effects. However, no post-test
399	                          improvements were noted with respect to the COD and speed tests in this group (i.e., the
400	                          asymmetries were reduced during jumping, but the players did not become faster).
401	                                Overall, the efficacy of training programs designed to decrease interlimb asymmetry
402	                          are heterogeneous [11–13]. Even when training programs reduce interlimb asymmetry
403	                          with a concomitant increase in the performance of the selected tests (e.g., CMJ and 10 m
404	                          sprint), the findings are often mixed [12]. It is also possible that the findings are neglecting
405	                          an important confounder: the ceiling effect [14,53,89]. The “weaker” limb may be further
406	                          from its maximum capacity, being more sensitive to training stimuli and showing greater
407	                          improvement than the “stronger” limb [14,89]. This could result in reduced interlimb
408	                          asymmetry, and is even more likely to occur in the case of already injured athletes [53].
409	                          Beyond that, the previously mentioned problems with the reliability of test–retest assess-
410	                          ments of lower limb asymmetries and with only analyzing the average values (thereby
411	                          neglecting to account for the interindividual variability) limit our understanding of how
412	                          well such programs work on an individual level. Additionally, the aforementioned training
413	                          programs mostly used standardized physical tests. The few sport-specific assessments were
414	                          performed under very analytical conditions. Therefore, it is unclear whether any reductions in
415	                          interlimb asymmetry were positive or desirable for enhanced athletic or sporting performance.
416	
417	                          2.3. What Does This All Mean?
418	                                 The sum of these findings shows that interlimb asymmetries are an intrinsic part of
419	                          high-level performance, even in supposedly more symmetric actions, and the effects of
420	                          training interventions on asymmetry and their consequences for performance are unclear.
421	                          Still, it is possible to speculate that even if it was established that asymmetries contribute
422	 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                           8 of 18

424	
425

427	                          positively to sports performance, they could produce a trade-off, increasing injury risk [90].
428	                          That is the subject of the next section.
429	
430	                          3. Asymmetry Is Not Necessarily Related to Injury Occurrence
431	                                Expressions such as “injury risk” and “injury prevention” bring about complex con-
432	                          cepts such as “predictors” of injury. Prediction requires that a prospective study ascertains
433	                          a relationship between the parameter and injury occurrence, and that a causal relationship
434	                          is established. Furthermore, for those causal relationships to be interpreted as predictive,
435	                          they must be replicated and exhibit a good fit in different samples. Commonly, all we have
436	                          are relationships established for a specific sample after the injuries have occurred. More
437	                          detailed accounts of this debate can be found elsewhere [91–93]. For the remainder of the
438	                          manuscript, we will refer to injury occurrence instead of injury risk.
439	                                It is intuitively accepted that injuries may cause increased asymmetries [45,53,94],
440	                          while it is not so clear that pre-existing asymmetries increase injury occurrence. Therefore,
441	                          observational studies comparing healthy versus injured or previously injured subjects are
442	                          potentially misleading, as they easily invite the readers to invert causality, even when
443	                          the authors state that only an association was measured. Severe injuries (such as muscle-
444	                          tendinous ruptures) are likely to increase the naturally occurring asymmetries in athletes,
445	                          resulting in excessively large interlimb asymmetries, owing to the fact that one limb is
446	                          incapacitated [53]. Hence, we understand the attempt to minimize such asymmetries
447	                          during rehabilitation and return to sport or return to play processes [53]. Regardless, we
448	                          question if fixed, arbitrary interlimb symmetry thresholds should always be achieved,
449	                          as was previously discussed. Unfortunately, several studies relate asymmetries to injury
450	                          occurrence without even providing basic associative data [1–10], potentially due to a
451	                          reliance on pre-conceived assumptions and beliefs on the subject. For example, in a
452	                          previously mentioned study whereby athletes performed a drop jump task [1], the potential
453	                          implications of the landing asymmetries towards injury occurrence were discussed at length.
454	                          However, this study did not directly assess injury occurrence, and so such asymmetries
455	                          are merely the realization of a fact and should not be used to infer subsequent injury
456	                          occurrence. In this section, we will delve into observational studies first, and prospective
457	                          studies second.
458	
459	                          3.1. What Observational Studies Really Say about Bilateral Asymmetry and Injury Occurrence
460	                               In professional soccer and basketball athletes with unilateral chronic ankle instability
461	                          (CAI), there was interlimb asymmetry between the injured and non-injured feet in the
462	                          basketball athletes with respect to the vertical time to stabilization during the postural
463	                          sway upon landing with both legs (~1.3 s required for the injured foot), but not in the
464	                          soccer athletes [3]. The authors concluded that balance exercises should be provided to
465	                          basketball and soccer athletes to reduce recurrent ankle sprains. However, no assessment
466	                          of injury recurrence was provided and so these suggestions remain purely speculative.
467	                          In the previously cited study with high-level male and female judokas [4], interlimb
468	                          asymmetries in external rotation strength were normal and there was no an assessment of
469	                          injury occurrence. Nevertheless, the authors stated that prevention programs should apply
470	                          similar workloads on both upper limbs and attempt to achieve greater symmetry.
471	                               An association study with 33 badminton players (19 male and 14 female; 14.4 ± 1.2 years
472	                          of age) assessed interlimb asymmetries in upper and lower limbs through inertial mea-
473	                          surement units (IMUs) and compared those with injury history [44]. No significant upper
474	                          or lower limb asymmetries were detected for the previously bilaterally injured group.
475	                          Although significant asymmetries were shown for the non-injured (<10%) and for the
476	                          unilaterally injured group (>10%), the between-groups difference in the asymmetry mag-
477	                          nitudes was not statistically different. These results suggest that some degree of interlimb
478	                          asymmetry should always be expected and is not necessarily associated with injury occur-
479	                          rence. In the same vein, knee flexion and extension strength, hop distance, and vertical jump
480	                          height were compared between 47 athletes with ACL reconstruction and 46 non-injured

482	
483

487	                          to knee flexion maximal strength than the non-injured athletes (~17% vs. ~9% interlimb
488	                          asymmetry, respectively). No between-group differences were found with respect to the
489	                          interlimb asymmetry of the remaining three tests. For the jump tests, this is not surprising,
490	                          given that measures of distance and height often mask biomechanical and strategy-based
491	                          information [95,96]. Indeed, only a minority of athletes (24% in the non-injured group and
492	                          17% in the injured group) showed symmetric (i.e., <10% asymmetry) performances in all
493	                          four tests [45].
494	                                In soccer, a study showed that 15 young male players had significant plantar pressure
495	                          asymmetries (e.g., hallux, fifth metatarsal, and medial rearfoot), with greater pressures
496	                          applied using the non-preferred foot [6]. These asymmetries were not observed in the
497	                          15 matched controls. Despite the authors relating such asymmetries to the risk of stress
498	                          injuries (it is even in the title of the paper), injury occurrence was not directly assessed.
499	                          In a study with 159 professional soccer players, interlimb asymmetries in isokinetic knee
500	                          flexion and extension were unrelated to competitive level or a history of injuries [97]. Still,
501	                          the authors proposed prescribing exercise to correct for the observed asymmetries. With
502	                          regard to isokinetic assessments of the knee, interlimb asymmetries of 19.5–31.7% in the
503	                          knee extension strength and 36.6–51.2% in knee flexion have been shown for elite U16
504	                          male soccer players [47], but this study once again did not assess any relationships with
505	                          injury occurrence.
506	                                In 25 teenage cricket fast bowlers (16 with and 9 without lower back pain [LBP]), the
507	                          symmetry of the abdominal muscle morphology (i.e., the combined thickness of the external
508	                          and internal obliques and transversus abdominis) was actually associated with LBP [98],
509	                          while the players without LBP had a superior thickness of the abdominal wall contralateral
510	                          to the dominant upper limb (i.e., the healthy athletes were more symmetric). Possibly,
511	                          these functional asymmetries are the by-product of the repeated lateral flexion of the trunk
512	                          during fast bowling actions and this reinforces the concept that some sports may require
513	                          above-normal bilateral asymmetries to function in a given task [14,34], which has been
514	                          previously suggested in other sports as well [99].
515	                                One study asked 6 rowers with a history of back injuries and 19 non-injured rowers to
516	                          perform 30 strokes with maximal exertion in a rowing machine [100]; the lower limb GRF
517	                          asymmetries were not significantly different in the rowers with or without a history of back
518	                          injury [100]. In 12 professional runners, an association between interlimb asymmetries in
519	                          the ground contact times and the injury history of the lower limbs in the previous 24 months
520	                          was established for the 400 m distance, but not for the other distances (600 m, 800 m, and
521	                          1000 m) [33]. It was unclear whether such asymmetries induced increased injury occurrence
522	                          or were caused by previous injuries (i.e., ankle sprains, Achilles tendinopathy, and shin
523	                          tendinopathy) [33].
524	                                This is not to say that any degree of asymmetry is desirable, as it is possible that
525	                          when surpassing certain thresholds (subject to inter- and intraindividual variation) injury
526	                          occurrence may increase [60]. Patients with primary ACL reconstruction that underwent
527	                          6-month functional and isokinetic testing and a minimum 2-year follow-up were assessed
528	                          for a secondary ACL injury [101]. Of the 344 patients, 59 (17%) had a secondary ACL injury
529	                          ~5 years after the primary injury. The LSIs in isokinetic testing were significantly greater in
530	                          the re-injured group with respect to 60◦ /s knee extension and flexion. However, regarding
531	                          knee extension, both groups presented an interlimb asymmetry ≥18%, with only a 7%
532	                          between-group difference. For knee flexion, both groups presented interlimb asymmetries

535	                          single-leg hop and triple hop distances [101]. However, another study found an increased
536	                          degree of interlimb asymmetry in male athletes with ACL reconstruction (n = 26) versus
537	                          healthy controls (n = 22) [94], while interlimb asymmetries of 23% (single leg drop jumps)
538	                          and 17% (single leg vertical jumps) where registered in injured subjects, and only 0–2%
539	                          asymmetries were observed in healthy athletes.

                          flexion, single-leg vertical jump, and single-leg hop) were undesirable and should be
                          properly remedied [5], despite injury risk not being formally assessed in any capacity.
                                 This search for bilateral symmetry (which includes bilateral trunk asymmetries and
                          also interlimb asymmetries) seems to derive more from deeply held beliefs than from
                          empirical findings [14], and risks placing performance and injury prevention programs on
                          the wrong track. Incidentally, craniocaudal and dorsoventral asymmetries are promptly
                          accepted (i.e., people understand that we need one head on top and two feet on the bottom,
                          and that we have two eyes in front of the head but none in the back). Somehow, it is with
                          bilateral asymmetry in sport that some in our profession seem to struggle to appreciate.
                          However, there is hope: the 10th edition of the ACSM guidelines for exercise testing and
                          prescription makes no mention of symmetry in general exercise prescription [15], unlike
                          the 9th edition [16]. Across the entire 10th edition of the guidelines, the only reference
                          to symmetry is the suggestion of symmetrical and rhythmical movement for people with
                          athetoid cerebral palsy [15].
                                 Biologically, the healthy development of human embryos requires breaking several
                          symmetries, including dorsoventral and craniocaudal [17]; unsurprisingly, proper embry-
                          ologic developmental also requires breaking left–right symmetry in vertebrates, including
                          humans [17–21]. Consequently, human anatomy is abundant with bilateral asymmetries.
                          Despite an apparent external symmetry, there is considerable asymmetry in thoracic and
                          abdominal organs [19,21]. For example, the diaphragm is asymmetric, usually reaching
                          one rib higher on the right side (due to the influence of the liver) and one lumbar vertebra
                          lower on the right side (due to a longer pillar) [22]. The aorta (which is also asymmetric)
                          presses against the vertebral column and usually produces a slight thoracic curvature with
                          convexity towards the right side [22]. Many other asymmetries can be pinpointed with
                          respect to internal organs (e.g., the liver, heart, lungs, colon, pancreas, etc.), which are all
                          commonly known. However, there are many additional bilateral asymmetries in vascular
                          networks, the lymphatic drainage system, and neural pathways [22]. In some cases, nerves
                          not only traverse distinct paths on the right and the left side of the body, but they also
                          present histological differences, such as in the case of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in
                          humans [23,24].
                                 Importantly, bilateral anatomical asymmetries in humans extend to the upper and
                          lower limbs as well (e.g., widths, lengths, neuromuscular paths, the different number
                          of muscle bellies, and among many other features) and have been widely described in
                          the literature [22,25–29]. A recent review has synthesized interlimb asymmetries in the
                          hamstrings’ structure and functionality, highlighting that important intraindividual asym-
                          metries may exist (some of which are not changeable with training) [30]. Naturally, laterality
                          (i.e., a lateral preference for using one limb over the other in certain tasks) coupled with
                          interlimb anatomical asymmetries suggests that common activities such as walking and
                          running should result in significant interlimb asymmetries in gait (kinetic and kinematic) in
                          healthy populations and athletes [31–33], and that sports may actually require magnifying
                          certain asymmetries [14,34] (e.g., sports with highly unilaterally-biased actions).
                                 Given all the above, asymmetry seems to be part of nature and integral to human
                          biology and behavior. In sports, interlimb asymmetries are highly task- and metric-
                          specific [7,11,12,14,34–43] and so should be analyzed within proper context. The goal
                          of this narrative review was to provide an account on the role of asymmetry in sports,
                          focusing on its relationships with performance and injury occurrence. We chose to perform
                          a narrative review to deliver a broad and critical overview of these topics, focusing on key
                          concepts and trying to tell a compelling story.

                          2. Bilateral Asymmetry Is Ubiquitous in Sports Performance
                               Bilateral asymmetry (a broad term referring to bilateral trunk asymmetries or inter-
                          limb asymmetries) should be expected to be and is (probably) not even clinically relevant
                          below the arbitrary thresholds of 5–15% [5,7,11,44–47], with an emphasis on the arbitrari-
                          ness of such thresholds since they are task- and metric-specific [7,11,12,34–39,42,48–50]
 Symmetry 2022, 14, 1993                                                                                             3 of 18




                          and likely also individual-specific [42,49–53]. Laterality (including, but not limited to,
                          handedness, mastication, and eye dominance) is a well-established feature in the animal
                          kingdom, including humans, and has been shown to be associated with increased func-
                          tional performance [54–59]. Importantly, both limb dominance and preference may also be
                          task-specific [34]. Therefore, interlimb asymmetries should not be automatically associated
                          with performance impairments [14,36,60]. Team sports such as basketball, handball, or vol-
                          leyball, to name some notorious examples, may boost upper limb asymmetries due to their
                          highly specialized and differentiated demands, and the same could be said of racquet sports
                          such as tennis, padel, or badminton. In the case of the lower limbs, bilateral asymmetries
                          are the norm in both general populations and in athletes [12]. For example, in 38 male
                          adult soccer players, resting tensiomyography assessments showed significant interlimb
                          asymmetries [61]. The vastus medialis contraction time, rectus femoris sustained time and
                          half-relaxation time, and biceps femoris sustained time were greater in the dominant limb,
                          while vastus lateralis contraction time and delay time were greater in the non-dominant
                          limb [61].
                               Moreover, we should consider the “noisy” character of asymmetry and the inconsis-
                          tency of outcomes, whereby in test–retest studies the group mean asymmetry often appears
                          to be relatively stable, but the standard deviation (SD) of the mean is almost always very
                          large (i.e., 50–100% of the mean asymmetry value) [38,49,52,62]. In contrast to the mean,
                          when individual datapoints are considered, changes in asymmetry’s magnitude and direc-
                          tion are usually quite large [38,39,49,50,52,53,62–66], suggesting caution when interpreting
                          the mean value of any interlimb asymmetry data. In fact, interlimb asymmetries should
                          not even be considered “true” asymmetries if their value is equal to or smaller than the
                          inherent variability of any given test [42,53] (e.g., coefficient of variation and typical error
                          of measurement). Additionally, limb preference and limb dominance are not necessarily
                          coincident; we refer the readers to the work of Virgile and Bishop [34] for an exploration
                          of this topic. To truly elucidate the relevance of asymmetry in sports performance, we
                          must understand: (1) the occurrence and relationships of bilateral asymmetry with athletic
                          performance, and (2) the effects of training interventions on interlimb asymmetries.

                          2.1. Occurrence and Relationship of Bilateral Asymmetry with Athletic Performance
                                A recent systematic review showed that, among several populations (including
                          17 studies with athletes), inter-limb strength asymmetries ranged from near symmetry
                          to asymmetries larger than 15%, without clear relationships with independent performance
                          tasks (such as isokinetic dynamometry, jump tests, and seated shot put, among others) [46].
                          Furthermore, additional research has shown that in sports research, no clear-cut associa-
                          tions exist between bilateral asymmetries and performance [14]. In addition, any findings
                          from cross-sectional studies should be taken with a pinch of salt, since the relationships
                          between interlimb asymmetry (magnitude and direction) and performance are not neces-
                          sarily consistent across a sports season [34,39,42,63,64,67]. One study assessed the ground
                          reaction forces (GRF) of 13 plyometrics-trained subjects (23 ± 3 years, 8 male and 5 female)
                          after a 45-cm drop jump whereby the subjects had to change their lead leg (i.e., the leg
                          initiating the movement to step off the box) [1]. Upon landing, the lead leg generated
                          greater forces than the trail leg. Interestingly, pairwise comparisons showed that significant
                          interlimb differences occurred only when the right leg led the movement, with the right
                          leg making earlier ground contact and generating greater force and impulse than the left
                          leg. Limb symmetry indices (LSI) generally showed asymmetries ≥10% [1]. This shows
                          that even in a simple drop jump task (with low contextual interference), athletes exhibit
                          marked interlimb asymmetry in their performance. However, the drop jump height was not
                          assessed, and so it is unclear how the observed asymmetries impacted jump performance.

                          effect size of η2 = 0.03) in the dominant side in comparison with the non-dominant side, but
                          the same was not observed for internal rotation [4]. Asymmetries favoring the dominant

                          performed under very analytical conditions. Therefore, it is unclear whether any reductions in

                          2.3. What Does This All Mean?
                                 The sum of these findings shows that interlimb asymmetries are an intrinsic part of
                          high-level performance, even in supposedly more symmetric actions, and the effects of
                          training interventions on asymmetry and their consequences for performance are unclear.
                          Still, it is possible to speculate that even if it was established that asymmetries contribute

                          3. Asymmetry Is Not Necessarily Related to Injury Occurrence
                                Expressions such as “injury risk” and “injury prevention” bring about complex con-
                          cepts such as “predictors” of injury. Prediction requires that a prospective study ascertains
                          a relationship between the parameter and injury occurrence, and that a causal relationship
                          is established. Furthermore, for those causal relationships to be interpreted as predictive,
                          they must be replicated and exhibit a good fit in different samples. Commonly, all we have
                          are relationships established for a specific sample after the injuries have occurred. More
                          detailed accounts of this debate can be found elsewhere [91–93]. For the remainder of the
                          manuscript, we will refer to injury occurrence instead of injury risk.
                                It is intuitively accepted that injuries may cause increased asymmetries [45,53,94],
                          while it is not so clear that pre-existing asymmetries increase injury occurrence. Therefore,
                          observational studies comparing healthy versus injured or previously injured subjects are
                          potentially misleading, as they easily invite the readers to invert causality, even when
                          the authors state that only an association was measured. Severe injuries (such as muscle-
                          tendinous ruptures) are likely to increase the naturally occurring asymmetries in athletes,
                          resulting in excessively large interlimb asymmetries, owing to the fact that one limb is
                          incapacitated [53]. Hence, we understand the attempt to minimize such asymmetries
                          during rehabilitation and return to sport or return to play processes [53]. Regardless, we
                          question if fixed, arbitrary interlimb symmetry thresholds should always be achieved,
                          as was previously discussed. Unfortunately, several studies relate asymmetries to injury
                          occurrence without even providing basic associative data [1–10], potentially due to a
                          reliance on pre-conceived assumptions and beliefs on the subject. For example, in a
                          previously mentioned study whereby athletes performed a drop jump task [1], the potential
                          implications of the landing asymmetries towards injury occurrence were discussed at length.
                          However, this study did not directly assess injury occurrence, and so such asymmetries
                          are merely the realization of a fact and should not be used to infer subsequent injury
                          occurrence. In this section, we will delve into observational studies first, and prospective
                          studies second.

                          3.1. What Observational Studies Really Say about Bilateral Asymmetry and Injury Occurrence

                          soccer athletes [3]. The authors concluded that balance exercises should be provided to

573	                          Asymmetry and Injury Occurrence?
574	                               Beyond any possible associations between asymmetry and injury occurrence, it is
575	                          also important to understand if there is any sort of causal relationship between the magni-
576	                          tude of asymmetry and injury occurrence [53]. Specifically, it would be relevant to assess
577	                          whether interventions aimed to reduce bilateral asymmetries (interlimb asymmetries and
578	                          bilateral trunk asymmetries) achieve such reductions and demonstrate that these reductions
579	                          in asymmetry lead to decreased injury occurrence. Considering the previous discussions
580	                          in this manuscript, “reduced asymmetries” should be considered on a task-, metric-, and
581	                          individual-specific context [7,11,12,34–39,42,48–53]. The consequences of reducing asym-
582	                          metry may also interact with the absolute baseline values. For example, if an athlete
583	                          has a stable 30% interlimb asymmetry and a training intervention reduces it by 50%, the
584	                          reduction from 30% to 15% asymmetry may have a certain impact on injury occurrence
585	                          (whether that impact is good or bad is another story). The same 50% reduction would not
586	                          be expected to have an impact if the absolute asymmetry was reduced from 4% to 2%.
587	                               Preferably, the interventions should be randomized, and the controls should perform
588	                          comparable interventions instead of being passive [106]. In Section 2, we explored the
589	                          findings of several interventions aiming to reduce interlimb asymmetry from an athletic
590	                          performance perspective [13,81–85,87,88,107], and a similar trend was evident for inter-
591	                          ventions relating to injury occurrence. As will become clear with the additional examples
592	                          below, it seems that studies implementing training interventions focused on reducing
593	                          bilateral asymmetries with the goal of reducing injury occurrence are not actually assessing
594	                          what they have proposed to. In other words, injury occurrence is not being assessed even
595	                          when the expression “injury risk” is in the title.

597	                          24 professional athletes (12 of which were controls) ~1 year after anterior cruciate liga-
598	                          ment (ACL) injury [2]. In this study (as in many others), the baseline values of interlimb

607	                          injury capacity may be a more relevant parameter [108]. What good is symmetry if an
608	                          athlete’s overall capacity is still 25% lower than their pre-injury levels? Returning to the
609	                          study on ACL recovery [2], the LSIs were assessed for single-leg hop and triple hop dis-
610	                          tances, as well as single-leg-landing kinetics before and after the 8-week intervention. While

613	                          sion, despite the more symmetric outcome measures, the GRFs were still asymmetrical [2].

615	                          the hop tests and therefore increased the readiness to return to sport [2]; however, since
616	                          there was no assessment of injury occurrence, it is unclear whether a more symmetrical
617	                          performance in the hop tests translated to a greater or smaller risk. In addition, distance is
618	                          an outcome measure and provides limited (or no) understanding of neuromuscular jump

622	                          completed a 6-week (12 sessions) intervention including bilateral unweighted squats and

626	                          intervention for both groups, while the biofeedback group exhibited significant decreases
627	                          in interlimb asymmetry with respect to the peak vertical GRF, but these decreases were not
628	                          maintained in a follow-up test session 6 weeks later (i.e., at week 12) [111]. This can be a
629	                          sign that the changes were fleeting and/or that there was a reduced repeatability of the
630	                          asymmetry scores, as previously discussed. Again, injury occurrence was not assessed in
631	                          this study [111].

643	                          only for an association between asymmetry and injury, without the support of causality.
644	                          Moreover, the reviewers highlighted inconsistencies in data collection and analyses, casting
645	                          doubt over their validity [113]. Another recent systematic review on the topic showed
646	                          highly inconsistent findings and suggested that no clear statement could be provided on
647	                          an eventual association between bilateral lower limb asymmetries and injury occurrence,
648	                          which was further complicated by the studies having used different operational defini-
649	                          tions of injury (i.e., injury mechanism, time loss, body part, and length of interventions
650	                          and follow-up) and different metrics to calculate interlimb asymmetry [40]. In addition,
651	                          even less is known regarding bilateral trunk or upper limb asymmetries (which would
652	                          be important, especially in sports that are highly asymmetric such as volleyball, water
653	                          polo, and others) and injury occurrence since most of the consulted literature focused on
654	                          the lower limbs. In summary, there seems to be no direct evidence from either observa-
655	                          tional or interventional studies to sustain the claims that interlimb asymmetries increase

663	                               Given that so many studies attempt to relate bilateral asymmetries with performance

667	                               errors (e.g., 5%) into the statistical analyses. Many asymmetries can possibly be

671	                               dividual responds to the same test on different sessions. If the individual changes
672	                               their asymmetry scores’ magnitude and, especially, direction, perhaps that test is
673	                               not appropriate for that individual and is providing misleading information. If the
674	                               changes in magnitude are inferior or equal to the test error, simply ignore it.

676	                               regarding the time of day and ambient temperature); otherwise, normal fluctuations
677	                               in an athlete’s performance in the test may be misinterpreted as noteworthy changes

679	                          4.   If an individual responds consistently to a given test, perhaps that test can be used to
680	                               assess the effects of a training intervention, or to assess how the scores change with
681	                               fatigue. However, even then, remember to analyze dose-response relationships and
682	                               perform retention tests where possible to determine how robust the changes are to a
683	                               detraining period.
684	                          5.   If the goal is to assess performance, make sure to assess the sport-specific performance,
685	                               preferably under competition-like conditions. Standardized physical tests or analytical
686	                               technical assessments may not be representative of performance during an actual
687	                               competition. Therefore, any asymmetry-related changes in performing standardized
688	                               testing should not be automatically transferred to sports-specific performance.

690	                               tionships. For example, can certain interventions reduce asymmetries, but also, does
691	                               such a reduction result in improved performance in the sport or key performance
692	                               indicators as well? Remember to factor items 1–4 when interpreting the findings from
693	                               such studies. These interventions should preferably include load-equated controls,
694	                               be randomized, and apply blind testing.

696	                               occurrence, make sure to adequately verify injury or reinjury rates. Otherwise, the
697	                               studies will remain speculative. Determining that certain athletes have bilateral
698	                               asymmetries (accepting these are true asymmetries) should not allow researchers to
699	                               suggest those asymmetries may increase injury occurrence.

701	                               training regimen most athletes are not getting injured. While performance can be
702	                               assessed frequently, assessing injury occurrences and gathering enough data to make
703	                               inferences require large samples and/or large time windows. Therefore, studies with
704	                               small samples and narrow periods of time should be very cautious when interpreting
705	                               injury-related findings.
