input.content:
{
 "id": "Q67",
 "sourceFile": "Where does blood flow restriction fit in the Toolbox of athletic development - A narrative review of the proposed mechanisms and potential applications.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Where Does Blood Flow Restriction Fit in the Toolbox of Athletic Development? A Narrative Review of the Proposed Mechanisms and Potential Applications' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Coaching", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of blood flow restriction (BFR) training in athletes, covering proposed mechanisms (anabolic signalling, ribosomal biogenesis, satellite cells, mitochondrial and angiogenic responses, fibre type) and applications. The authors report that low-load BFR resistance training increases muscle size similar to high-load training, with smaller strength gains and little change in power, while BFR combined with endurance or sprint work can improve local endurance and aerobic capacity. Cited athlete studies are mostly small.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search method is described, so the choice of studies cannot be checked. Many athlete data come from small samples, some outcomes are proxies such as girth or muscle thickness, and several recommendations in Table 1 extrapolate from untrained or non-athlete samples.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read BFR as a substitute for high-load training, which the authors explicitly reject as a replacement.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2023,
   "citation": "Davids CJ, Roberts LA, Bjørnsen T, Peake JM, Coombes JS, Raastad T. Where Does Blood Flow Restriction Fit in the Toolbox of Athletic Development? A Narrative Review of the Proposed Mechanisms and Potential Applications. Sports Medicine. 2023.",
   "doi": "10.1007/s40279-023-01900-6",
   "abstract": "Blood flow-restricted exercise is used as a low-intensity, time-efficient approach to gain many of the benefits of typical high-intensity training. This narrative review evaluates BFR as an additional training method for athletes, outlines its proposed mechanisms of action, and proposes how practitioners can use it alongside high-load training.",
   "tldr": "Blood flow restriction is a useful add-on for athletes, mainly for muscle size and local endurance, but it does not replace heavy training for maximal strength and power. Introduce it gradually to limit excessive muscle stress.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of the literature on BFR in athletes and trained individuals, with mechanistic and applied sections and a practical table of recommendations. The text does not describe a systematic search.",
   "findings": "Low-load BFR resistance training increased muscle size at a magnitude similar to high-load training, including in trained athletes, while strength gains were usually smaller. Conventional BFR had little effect on jump or sprint performance. High-frequency BFR blocks (five or more sessions per week) produced large increases in satellite cell numbers and myonuclei in cited studies, alongside transient fatigue and strength loss. Combined BFR and endurance work improved aerobic capacity and local endurance in cited studies.",
   "limitations": "The review is narrative, with no described search. Many cited athlete studies are small, some hypertrophy outcomes rely on girth or other proxies, and several mechanistic findings come from untrained individuals. The authors note that separate-session or block BFR has not been investigated in athletic cohorts and that hypertrophy responses to same-session BFR are unclear.",
   "practicalImplications": "Use BFR as a supplement to high-load training, not a replacement. Screen athletes first and introduce high-frequency blocks gradually, which the authors suggest early in pre-season and not close to competition.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: BFR can be added to strength and endurance blocks to build muscle size and local endurance at low loads, and high-frequency blocks may suit pre-season. Conventional low-load BFR does not appear to improve power or sprint performance, although some studies combining BFR with sprint or high-load work report gains, so keep high-load work in the programme.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review describes a four-step model from Loenneke et al. (BFR alone or with NMES or isometric work during immobilisation, then walking or cycling with BFR, low-load BFR resistance exercise, and finally high-load training) based mainly on rehabilitation studies. It does not test return-to-play criteria and should not be used as a validated return-to-sport protocol."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status": "CORRECTED",
   "changes": [
     "paper.findings: 'satellite cell activity' -> 'satellite cell numbers' ('increases in myogenic SC numbers that range from ~ 100 to 200%')",
     "paper.limitations: 'same-session or separate-block BFR in athletes has been studied little' -> separate-session or block BFR not investigated in athletes, same-session hypertrophy unclear ('Supplemental BFR in separate sessions or blocks has not been investigated in athletic cohorts'); replaced 'proxy or biopsy measures' with girth proxies and untrained samples",
     "paper.athleteDev: 'does not appear to add much to power or sprint performance' -> conventional low-load BFR only, since BFR with sprint or high-load work improved sprint and power in some studies ('additional benefits ... may be derived from combining BFR with high-intensity or high-velocity anaerobic training')",
     "paper.rtp: step 1 'isometric or NMES work' -> BFR alone or with NMES or isometric work during immobilisation, attributed to Loenneke et al. ('BFR alone (without exercise) can reduce the amount of muscle atrophy')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns": "",
   "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q71",
 "sourceFile": "Why Exercise may be Beneficial in    Concussion Rehabilitation- A Cellular Perspective.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective' matches the filename; the text is an accepted manuscript version.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of concussion pathophysiology (ion dysregulation, energy crisis, impaired neurovascular coupling) and of cellular signalling pathways (BDNF, CREB, mTOR, PGC-1a) that mild exercise may influence after concussion. The authors argue that mild, sub-symptom exercise introduced early may support recovery, while noting that higher intensity may be harmful. They cite human studies in which absolute rest was not better than usual care with progressive activity, and note that several human studies infer autonomic dysfunction from proxy measures.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search is described, and the cellular argument is largely theoretical, supported by mouse data and indirect human measures rather than measured human cellular responses. The exercise dose estimates it cites come from other sources and are not tested here.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the mechanistic pathways as proof that early exercise speeds concussion recovery, when the review presents these links as theoretical and the dose as needing individual judgement.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2019,
   "citation": "Dech RT, Bishop SA, Neary JP. Why Exercise may be Beneficial in Concussion Rehabilitation: A Cellular Perspective. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2019.",
   "doi": "10.1016/j.jsams.2019.06.007",
   "abstract": "Concussion diagnosis and rehabilitation have become a prevalent area of research, and exercise is now introduced earlier in recovery. This review aims to refresh the knowledge of concussion from a neurometabolic and broader physiological perspective, using gene expression to show why and how physical activity may optimise recovery at the cellular level.",
   "tldr": "Mild, sub-symptom exercise introduced early after concussion may support recovery through cellular signalling, but these links are largely theoretical and too much intensity may be harmful. Use the paper to inform clinical thinking, not as a tested exercise protocol.",
   "methods": "Narrative review of concussion pathophysiology and the cellular signalling pathways linked to exercise, with some human and animal studies cited. The text does not describe a systematic search.",
   "findings": "The review describes concussion-induced ion dysregulation, energy crisis and impaired neurovascular coupling, and argues that exercise-related pathways (BDNF, CREB, mTOR, PGC-1a) are active in both exercise and concussion. In a cited mouse study, BDNF did not change with exercise in the first 72 hours but increased at 14 to 20 days. Cited human work includes a trial in which home exercise at 80% of the treadmill symptom-threshold intensity shortened recovery compared with stretching, and studies in which absolute rest was not better than usual care with progressive activity.",
   "limitations": "This is a narrative review with no described search, and the authors call their rationale technically theoretical. Most human autonomic data are proxy measures, and the cellular evidence for exercise timing comes from mouse studies. The text is an accepted manuscript version, so pagination and volume are not printed.",
   "practicalImplications": "Early, mild, sub-symptom activity is favoured over absolute rest in the review's framing, while the acute phase is still described as a time for rest. The review cites estimates of 10 to 15 minutes at 40 to 50% of maximal heart rate for untrained and 15 to 20 minutes at 60 to 70% for trained individuals, and suggests moderate or higher intensity and sessions over 45 minutes may hinder recovery, but these come from other sources and need clinical supervision.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Not applicable. The paper concerns post-concussion exercise, not training prescription for healthy athletes.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review supports introducing mild, sub-symptom exercise early in concussion recovery, not full training. Its cited heart-rate and duration estimates are not return-to-play criteria, and it provides no new outcome or safety data to set clearance thresholds."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status": "CORRECTED",
   "changes": [
     "evidenceSummary: 'absolute rest did worse than usual care' -> 'absolute rest was not better than usual care' ('absolute rest ... has not resulted in a positive outcome as compared to \"usual care\"')",
     "paper.practicalImplications: 'The review does not give a dose, duration or intensity' -> reports the cited estimates ('10 - 15 minutes at 40 - 50% of heart rate maximum in untrained individuals, and 15 - 20 minutes at 60-70% ... in trained individuals') and the caution on moderate or higher intensity and sessions over 45 minutes",
     "paper.rtp: 'gives no dose-response or athlete safety data' -> cited estimates exist but are not clearance criteria",
     "screeningLimitations: 'animal and in vitro work' -> theoretical rationale with mouse data ('While the above is technically a theoretical rationale'); removed claim that no dose thresholds are given",
     "paper.findings: added the mouse BDNF timing result and the Leddy treadmill trial ('home activity at 80% of the initial assessment intensity ... more beneficial in time to recovery as compared to a stretching group')",
     "evidenceSummary and paper.tldr: added the authors' warning that higher intensity may be harmful ('Exercise can be harmful ... if exercise is too intense')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns": "Clinically sensitive concussion content. The heart-rate prescriptions are reported second-hand from reference 60 and should not be used as a protocol without checking the primary source.",
   "spotCheckPriority": "high"
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q73",
 "sourceFile": "Why should athletes brake fast - Influence of eccentric velocity on concentric performance during countermovement jumps at different loads.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Influence of Eccentric Velocity on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps at Different Loads' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Randomised within-participant laboratory study in 13 well-trained young men who performed loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM under four eccentric tempos: 5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated (consecutive jumps). The fast and accelerated tempos gave more eccentric work in the last 100 ms and higher peak and mean propulsive velocity than the 5 s and 2 s tempos, with no difference between fast and accelerated in concentric outcomes. The difference in end-eccentric work between the 5 s and accelerated conditions correlated with the difference in early concentric force (r = .774 to .880).",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, and no training adaptation was measured, so it cannot show whether fast eccentrics improve strength or power over time. The accelerated condition used consecutive jumps with no rest, whereas the other tempos had a 3-second rest, so the conditions differ in more than eccentric speed. The sample is resistance-trained men, not described as competitive athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read this as a rule that all loaded jumps should be braked as fast as possible for better training outcomes, when the study measured acute jump performance in one session only.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Hernández-Davó JL, Sabido R, Omar-García M, Boullosa D. Why Should Athletes Brake Fast? Influence of Eccentric Velocity on Concentric Performance During Countermovement Jumps at Different Loads. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2024 (ahead of print).",
   "doi": "10.1123/ijspp.2023-0273",
   "abstract": "The study compared four eccentric tempos (5 s, 2 s, as fast as possible, and accelerated) on eccentric kinetics and kinematics and on the concentric performance of loaded countermovement jumps at 30, 50 and 70% of 1RM in 13 well-trained participants.",
   "tldr": "In this single session, faster eccentric phases in loaded jumps increased end-eccentric work and jump velocity compared with slower tempos. Treat this as a reason to trial fast eccentrics and monitor the result, not as a settled training rule.",
   "methods": "Randomised, within-participant repeated-measures design. Thirteen well-trained young men completed 12 sets (four eccentric tempos by three loads) of four loaded countermovement jumps after 1RM testing and two familiarisation sessions. Barbell kinematics and kinetics were recorded with a linear position transducer, and a two-way MANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests was used.",
   "findings": "The accelerated tempo produced greater total eccentric work than all other tempos at each load. Eccentric work in the last 100 ms was greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s and 2 s tempos at each load. Early concentric force, peak velocity and mean propulsive velocity were greater in the fast and accelerated tempos than in the 5 s and 2 s tempos, with no differences between fast and accelerated. Eccentric depth did not differ by tempo or load. The change in end-eccentric work from the 5 s to the accelerated condition correlated strongly with the change in early concentric force (r = .774 to .880).",
   "limitations": "This is a single-session acute study in 13 men, with no training outcome. The accelerated condition used consecutive jumps without rest, unlike the other tempos, which confounds tempo with rest structure. The methods text refers once to a squat jump exercise, while the title, abstract and most of the text describe countermovement jumps.",
   "practicalImplications": "In this session, a fast or continuous eccentric phase in loaded jumps gave more end-eccentric work and higher jump velocity than slower tempos. Whether this improves strength or power over a training block is not tested here, so trial it and monitor it rather than adopt it as a fixed rule.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Faster eccentric phases (fast or accelerated) raised end-eccentric work and jump velocity in well-trained men within one session. Coaches could trial fast eccentrics in loaded jumps, but the chronic effect on strength and power was not measured.",
   "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Not applicable. The study used healthy trained men and excluded those with joint injury in the prior 12 months, so it does not inform rehabilitation or return to sport."
 },
 "verification": {
   "status": "CORRECTED",
   "changes": [
     "populations: 'Male Athletes' -> 'Adult / Recreational' (sample is '13 well-trained young men' with at least 3 years of resistance training, not described as athletes; the draft's own screeningLimitations said so)",
     "evidenceSummary and paper.findings: added that fast and accelerated did not differ in concentric outcomes ('No significant differences were found between the Fast and Accelerated conditions') and that both exceeded the 2 s tempo",
     "evidenceSummary and paper.findings: correlation described as within the accelerated condition -> delta between 5 s and accelerated conditions (Table 4 'Delta (5-Second vs Accelerated Condition)'), r = .774 to .880",
     "synthesisCaution: removed 'the accelerated tempo also changed rest' as the main caveat, since the fast tempo with rest gave the same concentric gains"
   ],
   "residualConcerns": "",
   "spotCheckPriority": "normal"
 }
}

 "primaryDomain": "Training & Performance",
 "domains": ["Training & Performance", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Sports Medicine", "Coaching", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of bilateral (interlimb) asymmetry in sport, covering its occurrence, its relationship with performance, its link to injury, and the effect of training on it. The authors report that asymmetry is common across sports, ages, sexes and competitive levels, is task- and time-dependent and poorly correlated with performance, and that no direct evidence shows pre-existing asymmetry causes injury or that reducing asymmetry improves performance.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search method is described, so the selection of studies cannot be checked. Much of the cited evidence is cross-sectional or uses standardized tests rather than sport-specific performance, as the review itself notes. The no-harm conclusion therefore relies partly on absence of evidence.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as saying asymmetry never matters, when it says asymmetry is poorly understood for sport-specific performance, that injuries tend to increase it, and that harmful thresholds may exist for some individuals.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2022,
   "citation": "Afonso J, Peña J, Sá M, Virgile A, García-de-Alcaraz A, Bishop C. Why Sports Should Embrace Bilateral Asymmetry: A Narrative Review. Symmetry. 2022;14:1993.",
   "doi": "10.3390/sym14101993",
   "abstract": "The paper critically reviews the evidence on the occurrence of bilateral asymmetry in sport and its effects on sports performance, injury risk and training, and it argues against assumptions that asymmetry is harmful.",
